speakeroldname: Righi Hon. L. S. St. Laurent (Prime Minister) moved:
speakerposition: Prime Minister; President of the Privy Council
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext: That on Wednesday, November 2 next, and every Wednesday thereafter to the end of session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
subtopic: PRECEDENCE OF GOVERNMENT BUSINESS ON WEDNESDAYS
speechtext:
Before this motion is put, Mr. Speaker, I should like to make a suggestion for which I believe there will be general support from members in all parts of the house.
I think that all who carry the appellation "private members" are grateful for the extent to which we have been granted our rights as private members during the course of this session. In fact we have had more private members' days, both with respect to private members' resolutions and with respect to public bills, than has been the case since before the war. Because of that fact I do not think the government can be criticized for suggesting that it is time they should take Wednesday afternoons. Nevertheless one of the questions that could come up on a Wednesday afternoon is of interest to all members of the house and of great interest throughout the country. I refer to the motion which was under discussion a week ago last Wednesday, having to do with federal aid to education. As a matter of fact when that debate was

Business of the House interrupted-and I point out that it was interrupted, not adjourned-the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) was speaking; and from his remarks it would seem that he expected, as certainly the rest of us expected, there would be another opportunity for hon. members to speak to that very important question.
It is an easy matter to word an amendment to the motion which would have the effect of giving us just one more Wednesday, and also the effect of putting the order for resumption of the debate having to do with education at the top of the list for that Wednesday. In order to achieve this dual purpose-which, as I say, I am sure will meet with general support-I move, seconded by my colleague the hon. member for York South (Mr. Noseworthy):
That the motion be amended by inserting therein, immediately after the words "November 2 next," the following words:
"notwithstanding the provisions of standing order 15, public bills and orders shall have precedence over notices of motion, and that on Wednesday, November 9,-"
If my amendment should carry, the motion would then read in this way-and I think I should put it on record so that the effect of the amendment will be clearly understood:
That on Wednesday, November 2 next, notwithstanding the provisions of standing order 15, public bills and orders shall have precedence over notices of motion, and that on Wednesday, November 9, and every Wednesday thereafter to the end of the session, government notices of motions and government orders shall have precedence over all other business except introduction of bills, questions by members and notices of motions for the production of papers.
As I have said already, the amendment would accomplish two purposes. In the first place it would give us one more Wednesday as a private members' day. It would put off the application of the Prime Minister's motion until Wednesday, November 9. In the second place it would reverse the order as between public bills and orders, on the one hand, and notices of motion, on the other, for next Wednesday, so that the first order to be called then would be the item at the top of the list of public bills and orders, which reads:
October 19-Resuming debate on the motion of Mr. Knight:
That, in the opinion of this house, the government should take into consideration means of expanding and equalizing educational opportunity across Canada, by the granting of financial assistance to the various provinces for that purpose.
I think it is generally agreed, Mr. Speaker, that one of the most interesting debates this session, and one most lacking in partisanship, was the one on this subject which took place on October 19. Hon. members in all parts of the house have been made aware of the nation-wide interest in this question by the telegrams and communications they have

received. We should like to hear the rest of the Prime Minister's speech; and I feel that it would be meeting the wishes of the house if the government were to accede to this amendment. I do not believe it is the sort of thing that should be made an issue, in terms of something we must fight about at this time. If I am wrong, if hon. members in all parties do not agree with me, that is the end of it. But I am sure the subject to which I refer is one in which we are so keenly interested that hon. members will want to support the amendment.
I want to make it clear that even I would not have the nerve to ask for further Wednesdays in blank form merely in order that we might go through the various motions standing on the order paper. But having regard to the importance of this subject, and the wide interest taken in it, I hope the government will consider granting us one more Wednesday for this purpose.
Before I sit down I wish to call the Prime Minister's attention, if it has not been done already, to the fact that he was paid a well-deserved compliment on page 4 of the current issue of Toronto Saturday Night, where it is pointed out that he has shown himself this session ready to accept good suggestions from the opposition.

Mr. Speaker, I hope that I may still obtain sufficient marks from the house, even if I do not succumb today to the cajoling flattery of the hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Knowles). The hon. member recognizes that during this session more time has been given to these interesting academic debates than was given to them in any session since before the war, and that notwithstanding the fact that when they came here on September 15 most hon. members hoped that the session would be short, though they knew there was quite a large volume of public business to be transacted. They know now that there is still a large volume of public business to be transacted.
The hon. member proposes that the rights some fifteen hon. members would have under the standing orders, to debate matters which

they consider of great interest, be taken away and that priority be given to the continuation of the debate-having to do with a very interesting subject, it is true-on a motion made by the hon. member for Saskatoon (Mr. Knight). Hon. members will realize that unless we sit until next summer there is little prospect of the hon. member's motion being reached again, unless we take away the rights given by the rules to the fifteen other members who have resolutions under the heading of notices of motions. Though the subject matter of the resolution of the hon. member for Saskatoon is extremely interesting, I am sure that there are other members who feel that the matters they propose to bring before the house, if and when they have an opportunity of doing so, are also interesting. I do not think that it would be a good precedent to have the house decide that any one of these academic resolutions submitted by hon. members should have precedence over the other. The rights of each member are equal, and when there is an opportunity for those rights to be exercised, it seems to me that they should be exercised according to the provisions of the standing orders.
This being so, I believe if it is proper that we should now take the time that would otherwise be given to these academic discussions and devote it to the transaction of urgent government business which has to be accomplished before we can reach prorogation, it should be without any qualifications. There should not be a day especially set aside for the continuation of the debate on the resolution of the member for Saskatoon.
This does not mean that the subject cannot be discussed in the house. Hon. members who are interested in discussing it know that, for instance, in the budget debate there is wide latitude as to the subjects hon. members may discuss. At various times discussion on the estimates provides ample opportunity for discussion of matters of this kind. I believe that the interest of each one of us in educa-cational matters, as well as in properly safeguarding the rights and jurisdictions of provincial governments, can be discussed.
So far as I am concerned I am quite content with the four minutes' participation I had in the debate a week ago last Wednesday, and am willing to reserve for some other time any further remarks I might have to make on the subject. I therefore feel that we cannot accept the suggestion of the hon. member. I hope that we shall not have to have a recorded division on the amendment.

I had hoped that when the Prime Minister saw fit to take part in the debate on the motion of the member for Saskatoon we might have some indication from him that he recognizes the importance of this matter and is prepared to meet those whom he described last night as "those dear provincial premiers". DEPARTMENT OF TRANSPORT 453. Departmental administration, $836,737.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: At the close of the previous sitting we were considering item 453. If I recall correctly, the hon. member for St. John's East had not completed his remarks. He may do so now.

When we adjourned some nights ago I was referring to the desirability of the establishment of a coastguard for Canada, and I was referring to the need of it in our own province of Newfoundland. I had remarked that the main industry of Newfoundland is fishing, and that a natural ancillary of that fishing industry is the use and operation of small boats. In view of the extreme changes in weather that we have at various times of the year, and with our extended coast line, which at various places is a rough one with little protection in the way of harbours, I submit that the establishment of a coastguard service is of the utmost importance to the province of Newfoundland.
Supply-Transport
I should like to refer you, Mr. Chairman, and hon. members, to an editorial in the Halifax Chronicle-Herald, of August 27, 1949. It reads as follows:
It was in the morning news yesterday:	The
United States coastguard cutter Coos Bay cleared Halifax harbour early today heading into the choppy Atlantic on a mercy dash to the liner Parthia.
A doctor, a portable respirator and a converter were flown to Dartmouth (just across the harbour from Halifax) by an American coastguard plane "after the Parthia sent out a plea for assistance" for a passenger suffering from infantile paralysis. The doctor and equipment were rushed across Halifax harbour from Dartmouth aboard the cutter which had been ordered into Halifax to make the final mercy dash. The United States coastguard cutter immediately headed into the Atlantic toward the Parthia.
It is what newspaper people call a great human interest story. But it is more than that. It is still another demonstration of the efficiency and value of the United States coastguard service . . . and of our own lack of such a service.
For Canadians it is not a pleasant spectacle-the spectacle of all this activity in the very port upon which a major part of the organization of a Canadian coastguard service should be based for operations in Atlantic waters; all this activity of a coastguard service that is not Canadian at all, but upon which we rely for the performance of much of the work which we should be doing for ourselves.
(And the Parthia, let it be remembered, is not an American ship.)
Through the years running into decades we have been indebted to the United States coastguard service for a thousand and one aids to our ships and shipping, promptly rendered and capably performed. While it is highly creditable to the United States, it is humiliating to Canadians that their own country should persist in this reliance upon the services of another country. It does something to Canadian pride, Canadian dignity.
I quote this editorial, which is couched in language much better than I could use, so that hon. members may understand, even those whose constituencies do not touch on the sea or on the great lakes, that this is a matter which concerns the dignity of this nation. It is about time that we asserted the dignity that the world expects of us.
So that hon. members may be aware of the history, the functions and the duties of the United States coastguard, I shall detail them as briefly as possible.
Alexander Hamilton, first secretary of the United States treasury, recognized the need of a floating police service as part of the national fiscal organization and in 1789 congress passed an act regulating the collection of duties on vessels and imported goods. In the following year, construction of revenue cutters was authorized. The service, however, never had a statutory designation, and was variously known as the revenue cutter service, the system of cutters, revenue marine, revenue marine service, and even revenue service.

Supply-Transport
In 1915 the lifesaving service was combined with the revenue cutter service to form the United States coastguard. In 1939 the bureau of lighthouses was transferred to the coastguard, and in 1942 the functions of the bureau of marine inspection and navigation were transferred to the service.
The United States coastguard is really part of the navy in war and of the treasury department in time of peace. The coastguard has grown to be a sea-going handy man having an interest in safety of travel on or over the sea as well as protecting federal interests at sea.
I shall detail for hon. members as briefly as I can the major functions of the United States coastguard. They are as follows:
Lifesaving stations all along the United States coasts; aids to navigation, consisting of lighthouses, buoys, radio beacons, radar beacons, and the tenders and personnel to maintain them; Loran-the new electronic navigation system used by ships and four out of five transatlantic air lines; direction-finder stations publications, such as notice to mariners; patrolling cutters: weather stations and plane guard at sea, probably to expand to thirteen in north Atlantic, as recommended by PICAO; rescue cutters; federal functions in Greenland; federal functions in Alaska: air-sea rescue; coordinating agency, maintaining continuous record of all vessels and planes at sea, thereby facilitating expeditious rescue in case of emergency; communications system-radio networks over all United States teritorry, telephone system completely covering United States coast line; merchant marine inspection and safety: supervision of safe construction and outfitting of all merchant ships. United States; supervision of safe operation by regular inspections and checking for proper maintenance of safety devices.
Who knows, Mr. Chairman, that if we had a Canadian coastguard service and one of its functions was the inspection of all safety devices on ships, what might have happened in the case of the Noronicl Who knows if that awful tragedy might have been averted if we had a Canadian coastguard service? I continue with the list:
Licensing and certificating of merchant marine personnel, and discipline of merchant marine personnel; international ice patrol: keeping track of ice in north Atlantic during ice-menace season, issuing appropriate warning; icebreaking in harbours and great lakes: prevention of smuggling; flood relief; miscellaneous: enforcement of provisions of Alaska seal treaty; enforcement of provisions of international whaling treaty; enforcement of harbour pollution act, fishing laws, transportation of federal representatives, mails.
That is a long list of the duties performed by the United States coastguard service. I ask, Mr. Speaker, is it possible for a police force, no matter how good it may be-and the Royal Canadian Mounted Police have a record second to none as a police force-to discharge the duties I have just enumerated? The coastguard is a sea service, a service for seamen, a service that cannot be undertaken by a land based force or a force which is really the minor wing of a land force, no

matter how good that force may be. I therefore respectfully submit that the necessary steps should be taken immediately to set up a proper and efficient coastguard service for Canada, a service that would be able to take care of the many and varied duties that only a service of that kind can perform, a service of which in the years to come all Canadians might be justly proud.
When the question of saving life is at stake, cost should not be considered. For the sake of economy, for the sake of national pride, for the sake of humanity, we should have a coastguard service equipped and manned for the numerous sea-going duties now undertaken by the United States coastguard service. Too long have we let Uncle Sam do our work. It is about time that we did it ourselves.
In conclusion I trust that I will be pardoned for giving the committee a little poem from the official book of the United States coastguard, entitled, "The United States Coast-Guard-its History, Vessels, and Doctrine". The poem is entitled, "Coastguard Cutter ', and reads as follows:
When she steams into the harbour People don't flock 'round like bees;
For she ain't no grim destroyer.
No dark terror of the seas.
And there ain't a load of romance To the guy that doesn't know.
In a ship that just saves vessels When the icy northers blow.
But the men that sail the ocean In a wormy, rotten craft,
When the sea ahead is mountains With a hell-blown gale abaft;
When the mainmast cracks and topples,
And she's lurching in the trough,
Them's the guys that greets the cutter With the smiles that won't come off.
When the old storm signal's flyin',
Every vessel seeks a lee,
'Cept the cutter, which ups anchor And goes plowing out to sea,
When the hurricane's a-blowin'
From the banks to old cape Cod,
Oh, the cutter, with her searchlight,
Seems the messenger of God.

Mr. Chairman, I wish to congratulate the hon. member for St. John's East upon having entered the lists in support of our contention that we should have a Canadian coastguard service. He did it exceptionally well, and as one who has been here for five years I will tell him that he might find it advantageous if he were just to put the speech away in mothballs for another year-because he will be able to pull it out again and use it next year, I am sure. It will be just as instructive then as it is now -and I congratulate him upon having made it.
I think that next year our Canadian seamen, if they get into trouble, will be singing "God Bless America"; and if they ever reach

the point where they cannot sing that, then they will have to sing "Nearer My God to Thee".
In what I say I am not critical of the Minister of Transport, because he runs a pretty good service, having in mind what we give him. He has a couple of lifeboats out on the Pacific coast. Of course they are small, and they cannot go anywhere in a big sea. They are pretty dangerous; if one got out in a big sea in one of those boats he would freeze to death-and if he happened to help anyone else, that person would perhaps freeze to death too. There is no radar on them; I hope there is a compass, although I am not sure. They do, however, perform a useful service, and are handled by capable men. They go out to service our lighthouses, at points where landings with supplies can be made only with small vessels. They look after the lights around the channels. I have no criticism at all of the service they are rendering out there. My only comment is that while they are useful adjuncts to a lifesaving service, they are not useful as a coastguard.
Last year I made a speech in the house on this subject. I pointed out to the minister that we could obtain vessels suitable for this purpose; that good vessels were still available from the United States navy for $15,000 which cost about $385,000 to build. They are equipped with aids to navigation, such as asdic, radar, and a 1,200 horse power diesel engine. I can assure the committee that they are extremely seaworthy-boats on which one could put a tow-winch, and, if a vessel were in difficulty, pass a line to it.
I feel that the coastguard in Canada is not something that should be under the Minister of Transport. In my view the Minister of National Defence should be the man to handle that problem. For some unknown reason this year the Department of National Defence saw fit to send two seaworthy ocean-going tugs and have them stationed alternately at Winter Harbour on the west coast of Vancouver island. They were given instructions to look for Japanese mines, and, if any showed up, they were to go out and destroy them. They were careful never to do anything constructive-and this is where I take exception to what is being done by the Department of National Defence. Any time we suggest to them that they do anything constructive in return for the $375 million or $400 million that is appropriated to them, and suggest that they provide us with rescue facilities along our coast line, they say: "Oh, no; we are destroying Japanese mines, and certainly we are not going to be useful to anyone."

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I point out that we are discussing item 453, Department of Transport-not the Department of National Defence.

Thank you, Mr. Chairman, for calling that to my attention. But the Minister of Transport gets so much abuse-and he is a very good friend of mine-that I sometimes feel that the abuse is not entirely justified. I was just pointing out through you, sir, that I think he should be making this speech himself, and saying that it is his colleague the Minister of National Defence who should be doing all this.
As I have pointed out, the Department of National Defence provided us with two vessels last year which, in extreme emergencies, could have acted as coastguard cutters. But when we got them up at Winter Harbour we found that evidently they had been told not to do anything, and they made very sure to follow out instructions carefully.
Perhaps I am reaching somewhat into the functions of the Department of National Defence, but I suggest that the Department of National Defence could provide the service for which we are asking. I cannot think of a better place to train young Canadian seamen than to put them on a boat 120 or 130 feet long, send them out to sea and teach them how to pay out a tow-line in a heavy sea if someone is in trouble. You do not make seamen by putting them in the aircraft carrier Magnificent and teaching them how to run an elevator. That is not the way to train them. To make sailors you have to get them into small boats. I suggest that the Minister of Transport talk to his colleague and see if he cannot sell him, not a bill of goods but something for the good of Canada. It seems to me that for the $375 million we are spending in the Department of National Defence we should have a coastguard service and get some real value for our money.

Mr. Chairman, the hon. member for Comox-Alberni, who is much closer to the inner circle of government than I am, has offered some comments which I am afraid will cause discouragement out on the Pacific coast, because many agencies out there had hoped that an improved coastguard service or sea-rescue service would develop during the forthcoming year.
I know that some improvements have been made in the matter of small vessels operated by the Department of Transport. These, as the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has said, spend most of their time in replenishing supplies and looking after aids to navigation around our coast. There has been, however, a growing demand in recent months for an adequate coastguard service along that coast.

Supply-Transport
Whether it should be under the Department of Transport or some other department may be a debatable point. At the present time, however, the Department of Transport is charged with the responsibility of looking after our shipping and of supplying aids to navigation, lighthouse services and all that sort of thing. Therefore I submit this is the appropriate time to raise the question of the need for a coastguard service.
I am glad the hon. member for Comox-Alberni has referred to the activities of the two small naval tugs stationed on the west coast of Vancouver island last summer. One of those tugs was asked by the R.C.A.F. to proceed to the rescue of a vessel in difficulty some 300 miles off the coast of Vancouver island. The tug proceeded but turned around and came back, the reason given, as stated in the News-Herald, of October 8, being that the captain of the vessel learned that a United States coastguard vessel was proceeding to the ship in distress, and also that there were numerous other fishing vessels in the immediate vicinity. Therefore the naval tug turned around and went back. Three days later the ship in distress was towed into harbour by a United States coastguard cutter. The suggestion that fishermen who are earning a livelihood on the sea, and who are exposed to the dangers of the Pacific, should have to leave their lawful occupation to stand by another ship seems fantastic unless the ship is in dire necessity and there is no other rescue vessel available.
As has already been said, there are many different government agencies and departments with ocean-going vessels on the Pacific coast that are in some measure responsible for protective service. There are fishery patrols, Royal Canadian Mounted Police vessels, hydrographic service vessels, ships of the Department of Transport, and so forth. There are also the sea rescue squads of the R.C.A.F. and the naval vessels, but they are not co-ordinated in spite of an effort that is being made to reach some degree of co-ordination.
It is essential, if effective rescue facilities are to be provided, that all these agencies be co-ordinated under one head, and that some individual have authority to order a government vessel to proceed to the scene of a wreck or to a ship that is in distress. That would seem to me to be one of the main functions of a coastguard service.
I know that to install a coastguard service in any way comparable with the most efficient service maintained by the United States would run into a great deal of money, perhaps more

money than the government would feel justified in expending at the present time. Nevertheless, with the resources that are now available, it should be possible to have these services co-ordinated to a higher degree than is the case at the present time, and thereby have a more efficient service. It should be possible for some individual to be able to order a government vessel of a different service, which may happen to be in the vicinity, to proceed to the scene of a marine disaster. Such power does not exist at the present time.
The R.C.A.F., which receives information about disasters, can advise a vessel of another department of that disaster, but they do not have power to instruct it to proceed to carry out rescue work. Without going to a great deal of expense to set up a complete coastguard service, I hope that the minister will look into the matter and see if it is not possible to achieve a higher degree of co-ordination of all these existing means-
That is the whole point.

-of rescuing life at sea. There is one other point akin to the question of a lifeguard service. In 1948 representatives of the Department of Transport attended an international convention concerned with the safety of life at sea. I believe they approved of the general agreements drawn up at that convention. These agreements are not to come into force until the first of January, 1951, but I believe there is a provision in them that they will only come into force on the 1st of January, 1951, provided that at least twelve months before that date not less than fifteen acceptances of the convention, including seven by countries each with not less than one million gross tons of shipping, have been deposited. I should like the minister to say whether an acceptance has been deposited by Canada, or whether Canada intends to endorse the agreement signed by her representatives before the first of January, 1950. That is the date by which it will be necessary for our acceptance to reach the international convention if we are to comply with the twelve months deadline prior to the 1st of January, 1951.

May I tell the hon. member immediately that Canada is a signatory to the convention and intends to accept it. I have not looked into the legal question as to whether or not it will be necessary before the next session of parliament to bring down a convention, or whether amendments to the Canada Shipping Act will suffice.
That would not be too late for it to be accepted by the 1st of January, 1951?
No.

I should like to place before the minister a matter of serious and direct concern to at least 5,000 of my constituents. I refer to the maintenance of an adequate and suitable steamer service on the Arrow lakes. I have mentioned this subject before. It is not a very glamorous one from a news reporter's point of view, but when I speak of this subject I think of the farmers, the fruit growers and the lumbermen of that district who make their living by hard work.
For the information of hon. members, in order that they may understand the situation existing at the present time, I think I should inform them where the Arrow lakes are and relate some of the history of the service. The Arrow lakes are an extension of the Columbia river running from Arrowhead, which is about 35 miles south of Revelstoke, to Castle-gar on the south, which is about 25 miles north of the international boundary, in all a distance of over 100 miles. The first service on the Arrow lakes and the upper Columbia was provided in 1865 when the steamer Forty-nine was used to transport miners' supplies and equipment to the Big Bend north of Revelstoke.
In 1894 several men incorporated what was known as the Columbia and Kootenay Steam Navigation Company, and proceeded to build several steamers, the first of which was the Columbia. Then they built the Lytton and the Kootenay. These steamers served to develop the district for a year until in 1895 the first stern-wheelers were built, the old Nakusp and the Trail.
In 1896 the service was taken over by the Canadian Pacific Railway. This company increased the fleet by building the Rossland and the Kootenay, later the Minto in 1898, and the steamer Bonnington in 1911. During the period from 1896 to 1911 there was ever-increasing traffic. I lived in the neighbourhood of that lake for the greater part of those years. This was the main artery of travel, giving people in the interior of British Columbia access to the coast. As a matter of fact the traffic increased to such an extent that the C.P.R. built the palatial steamer, the Bonnington, in 1911 to accommodate it; and a reference to the minutes of a directors' meeting of the Canadian Pacific Railway of that date indicates that this route was very profitable.
Then with the completion of the Kettle Valley railroad in 1916 the situation changed. From that time on the major portion of the traffic from the southeastern interior, both passenger and freight, was carried over this railroad to the coast. Since then passenger and freight traffic has gradually declined,
Supply-Transport
and finally brought about the decision to dispose of the Rossland, Kootenay and Bonnington, so that today all we have left of the fleet on the Arrow lakes is the 51-year-old stern-wheel steamer Minto. There are only two stern-wheelers operating in any province in Canada, as far as I know; one is the Moyia on the Kootenay lake and the other is the Minto on the Arrow lakes.
As the situation grew worse from year to year organizations in the lake district complained to government departments and to various officials, without result. During the period of the war the people decided to do the best they could with the service that was being given in the district; but since the war there has been an increasing demand from the residents of that area for an improved and continued service on the Arrow lakes, which demand has been stimulated during the last year by fears that in the near future the Canadian Pacific may turn over the service to other interests. Boards of trade, farmers' institutes, fruit growers' organizations and other associations in the area are united in wishing to see the service continued and improved by the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, because they are of the opinion that no other company could give a satisfactory service for the whole area.
When I was a member of the provincial legislature I used to receive resolutions from various organizations with respect to this matter. I brought it to the attention of the provincial government, where I was told that this was a matter of federal concern, that it had nothing to do with the provincial government. So when I arrived in Ottawa I took it up with various departments of government, including the Department of Transport. On the first occasion the minister told me that since these lakes were entirely within the confines of the province of British Columbia he was of the opinion that this service came under provincial jurisdiction. Now I want to read the minister's reply to a letter I wrote and a query of mine in the house during the latter part of 1947:
Dear Mr. Herridge,
When the estimates of my department were before the house you raised the question of the service being given by vessels operated by the C.P.R. on the Arrow lakes. You will remember you also wrote to me in the matter about the same time.
I placed before the board of transport commissioners your representations that the frequency of the service on the lakes should be increased both for the carriage of passengers and freight and also your suggestion that this service be brought under the operation of the Transport Act, and consequently under the jurisdiction of the board.
Section 12, subsection 4 of the act is, in part, as follows:
"The provisions of this part shall not apply in the transport of goods or passengers

Supply-Transport
(a) between ports or places in British Columbia".
The board have carefully reviewed the situation in the light of your observations, and have reached the conclusion that the operation of ships on the Arrow lakes does not lend itself to regulation under the Transport Act. Accordingly the board have expressed the view that the act should not be amended as suggested by you.
I felt I should inform you of the position taken by the board in this regard.
With best wishes.
That is signed by the minister.

If I may interrupt the hon. gentleman, Mr. Chairman, he has been permitted to go on for some time now, but my impression was that he was entirely out of order. In view of the letter he has just read, which clearly indicates that the board of transport commissioners have no jurisdiction in the matter and that in order to have jurisdiction the Transport Act would have to be amended, I submit with deference that this is not a subject which comes under the item now before the committee.

I think the minister is correct on that point, but that is not the point I am really going to make in concluding my remarks. I would like to read a letter I received from the secretary of the board of transport commissioners in reference to this matter, under date of May 19, 1949:
Dear Sir,
I have for acknowledgement your letter of May 10 addressed to the board's director of operation in the above noted connection.
That is, in respect to C.P.R. steamer service on the Arrow lakes.
I have been directed to state that the board is of the opinion that it has no power to prevent the disposal by the C.P.R. of its boat equipment to private interests and is therefore not in a position to assist in this matter.
That is signed by Mr. P. F. Baillargeon, secretary of the board. The point I wish to bring to the attention of the minister is that I have been told repeatedly this does not come under the jurisdiction of the federal parliament. I am of a different opinion, as I think a good many people are, and I am appealing to the house because under these circumstances we have no other recourse. I want to quote from the act of incorporation of the original company to prove that this steamer service does come within the jurisdiction of the parliament of Canada. I am referring to chapter 87, 53 Victoria, an act respecting the Columbia and Kootenay Railway and Navigation Company, assented to April 24, 1890. This is the preamble:
Whereas a petition has been presented stating that the Columbia and Kootenay Railway and Navigation Company has undertaken the works hereinafter described, and that it will facilitate its financial arrangements if it can lease such works to the Canadian Pacific Railway Company, and praying that authority so to do may be conferred by the

parliament of Canada; and it is expedient to grant the prayer of the said petition; Therefore Her Majesty, by and with the advice and consent of the Senate and House of Commons of Canada, enacts as follows.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I am sorry to interrupt the hon. member, but I think he is pursuing the discussion of a case which does not come under the item now before the committee. Following the remarks of the Minister of Transport on a point of order, the hon. member said he would come to a different conclusion and that he agreed with the point of order raised by the minister. I permitted him to continue his remarks, but I see he is still discussing the same case. So I would ask him to be kind enough to confine his remarks to the item before the committee; that is, departmental administration, Department of Transport.

This is the only opportunity I may have to prove that this steamer service comes within the jurisdiction of this parliament and that the department should do something about it, and I believe that properly comes under the item administration. I shall not be long, and as I am not in the habit of taking up the time of the house unnecessarily, I would like to proceed with my appeal to the minister and the committee.
I have heard the appeal before, but I have no objection to hearing it again if it pleases my hon. friend.

The minister is very kind, but I hope this appeal will bear more fruit than my former efforts. Section 2 provides:
The following works, being those which the company by its said act of incorporation is empowered to undertake, own and operate, are hereby declared to be works for the general advantage of Canada. . . .
This is the point I want to make.
. . . that is to say: A railway from the outlet of Kootenay lake, in British Columbia, through the Selkirk range of mountains, to a point on the Columbia river as near as practicable to the junction of the Kootenay with the Columbia river in that province. . . .
I am going to abbreviate as much as possible, but the act goes on:
Nothing herein contained shall be construed in any way to affect or render inoperative any of the provisions of the said act of incorporation which authorized the said company to undertake, own and operate the said works as aforesaid; but hereafter the same shall be subject to the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, and the provisions of the Railway Act.
I believe the act of incorporation clearly indicates, Mr. Chairman, that this steamship service is the concern of this parliament and should operate under the Railway Act or some other act coming within the jurisdiction of the minister.

I should like to consider the incorporation act in relation to clause 10 of section 92 of the British North America Act, which deals with the exclusive powers of provincial legislatures with certain exceptions. One of the exceptions is contained in clause 10 and reads as follows:
Such works as, although wholly situate within the province, are before or after their execution declared by the parliament of Canada to be for the general advantage of Canada or for the advantage of two or more of the provinces.
Surely my argument is sound.
I know that in recent years, Mr. Chairman, considerable losses have been incurred in the operation of these steamers. I have discussed the matter with the officials of the Canadian Pacific Railway as well as the officials of the Department of Transport. I found them all sympathetic in a general way but I am of the opinion that, as this service without doubt comes within the jurisdiction of this parliament and therefore under the Minister of Transport, consideration must be given to proposals for continuing it for the people affected.
I remember the early days when these people settled on the lakes. The Canadian Pacific and other companies sold land to many of them. They cleared the land, bought timber holdings and settled there on the assumption that the then satisfactory service would be continued. I do not think this government can blandly overlook the situation in which those people now find themselves.
I raised this question in 1947, as the minister mentioned. To him it is a repetition. After I heard a member of the Progressive Conservative party thanking the minister for a subsidy given a steamer which operated entirely on a lake situated within the province of Ontario, I asked the minister if he would give consideration to the granting of a subsidy for the service on the Arrow lakes. At that time he said yes.
In conclusion, Mr. Chairman, I am appealing to the minister to have his department investigate this situation to ascertain whether it is necessary to bring this service under the transport or other act. I suggest for the immediate future, a subsidy should be provided for the maintenance of the service and for its improvement. Not only do these steamers serve the towns, the isolated hamlets, lumber camps, fruit farmers, and residents along the lakes, but if the government has vision they can be of great value to Canada as a tourist attraction. I do urge that the minister have his department investigate this question and confer with the officials of the Canadian Pacific, the company concerned, with a view to granting a subsidy.
Supply-Transport
The minister is granting a subsidy of approximately $405,000 this year to steamships on the west coast. Will he say what he intends to do about these proposals?

The hon. gentleman who has just taken his seat will excuse me if I do not take up too much time replying to his request for consideration of the service on the Arrow lakes. The matter received considerable attention last year and was referred to the board of transport commissioners. After a careful investigation, they came to the conclusion it was a case which did not come within their jurisdiction. Furthermore, the board felt that the Transport Act should not be amended so as to bring this service within the jurisdiction of the act. I do not believe I can add very much to what was said then.
There is, of course, the question of the essentiality and convenience of the service to the public, which is another matter. The hon. member suggests that consideration be given to a subsidy. The maritime commission administers subsidies, and the owner of the service should make application to them, just as other steamship operators do. After a careful study of the facts and circumstances, if the maritime commission would recommend either that a subsidy is or is not warranted, if such an application is made then I believe my hon. friend will have gone as far as he can go in so far as the services over which I have any control are concerned. I do not believe he can expect much more than that. I shall be glad to facilitate the application of the owners of the service if they care to make one.
I should not like to leave the matter of the coastguard service without some general remarks in reply. I am grateful to the members for Comox-Alberni (Mr. Gibson), St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) and Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) for their contribution to this debate. The hon. member for Comox-Alberni was right when he said it is not the first time the matter has been up for consideration.
I wonder if the member for St. John's East realizes just how tremendous this problem is? This is a large country with an ocean on either side of it. It is not an easy matter to patrol our coasts and the great lakes as well. It is not a problem which can be solved merely by words, or by criticism of what is being done.
Some of the members of this house apparently do not realize how much we are doing. The member for St. John's East referred to the United States coastguard cutter coming to the assistance of a certain ship in the Atlantic region. That coastguard cutter forms part of the north Atlantic ice patrol, towards the maintenance of which Canada pays a

Supply-Transport
certain amount by virtue of an international agreement. When that cutter came to the assistance of our ship, it was a direct result of the contribution Canada made towards the cost of the ice patrol.
I could read to the house a statement of the number of casualties that have taken place on the east and west coasts, as well as the great lakes, and inform the house how many of those have been looked after by our own people, but the list is too long to put on the record. I should like to take one or two examples. In 1946-47 on the Pacific coast there were 120 casualties. Seventy-five of them needed no assistance and the remaining 45 were looked after exclusively by our own ships. In 1947-48, on the west coast again, there were 95 casualties, 60 of which needed no assistance and the remaining 35 were taken care of by our own ships.
Would the minister indicate what he means by "our own ships"? Does that include salvage vessels?

Yes, it would include ships of the Department of Transport, salvage vessels, fishing vessels and R.C.M.P. vessels.
On the west coast in 1948-49, there were 95 casualties, of which 62 required no assistance.
Mr. Chairman, would the minister explain what he means by "casualties"? It has a certain connotation, and when he says a casualty would require no assistance, what does he mean?
Casualty does not mean the loss of life. It would include a ship that is stranded at sea by reason of engine failure or a ship that has been rammed by another ship.
Then, "casualty" refers to ships and not persons.

Yes. Of the remaining 33 casualties in 1948-49 which required assistance, 32 were looked after by our ships and one by the United States coastguard. The same thing could be said of the east coast. By my remarks, I do not want to minimize in any way the value of the service rendered by the United States coastguard. I think on many occasions I have taken the opportunity to write to those who are in charge of this service in the United States, to thank them for the assistance they have given Canada. I can think of one particular occasion on the great lakes when they were of great service to us. I should not like anyone in the house to think that Canada is not extremely grateful for what is being done by the United States coastguard service. What

I want to bring to the attention of the committee is that Canada is doing something in this matter.
Will the minister be good enough to put on record the figures for the east coast operations?

Yes. On the Atlantic coast in the year 1946-47 there were 67 casualties, 55 of which required no assistance and 12 to which assistance was rendered-again by government vessels, by fishermen and salvage companies. In 1947-48, on the Atlantic coast, there were 98 casualties, 84 requiring no assistance and 14 requiring assistance, all of the 14 being looked after by our own vessels. In 1948-49, on the east coast there were 84 casualties, 53 requiring no assistance and 31 requiring assistance; 2 of the 31 were assisted by United States coastguard vessels. That completes the list to date for the Atlantic coast.
I think the problem is chiefly one of coordination. I think it was the hon. member for Comox-Alberni or the hon. member for Nanaimo who put his finger on the main point when he said that these facilities that we have on the east coast, on the west coast and on the great lakes might perhaps be brought together more than they are at the moment. Consideration is being given to the further co-ordination of these services, perhaps under the Department of National Defence, perhaps under the Department of Transport. I do not know which of the two departments is the better qualified. But in view of the seriousness of the problem a committee has been established by the government. This committee is composed of members of departments which are concerned, such as Mines and Resources, Fisheries, R.C.M.P., Transport and the three divisions of National Defence.
The object of this committee is to ascertain whether improvement can be made on what exists. I think the committee, for instance, will study what might be the maximum facilities, what would be the minimum, to meet the situation and what would be a middle position; and consider the possibility of coordination of all existing services under one head to establish responsibility for locating the vessels on the east coast, the west coast and the great lakes, for getting in contact with them, for keeping in contact with all government vessels, be they Transport vessels or those of other departments, and indicating to those vessels where a ship is in distress, and indicating how quickly the ship can be relieved, and matters of that kind.
To those members therefore who have interested themselves in this problem I can say that their efforts have not been in vain. I am not able to announce anything concrete

at this time but I think the committee will be pleased to know that an attempt at least is being made to study the problem and to see what the best possible solution is at this time.

I want to draw the minister's attention to the Canadian National Railway line which runs east from Edmonton to a point called Heinsburg. It so happens that this railway line runs through a thickly-populated farming area, but there is a gap of some 39 miles from Heinsburg to a point called Frenchman's Butte in Saskatchewan. The result is that the farmers' cost of production is considerably higher than it would otherwise be. I understand that the reason this line was not completed was the coming of depression years and the war.
Conditions have now changed. Quite significant developments have taken place along that line which I think are of importance to our Canadian economy. It so happens that along this line the famous Redwater oil field has been discovered. This is the largest field not only in Alberta but in Canada. Farther along the line there is a salt mine which has been developed only within the last year. The result is that there is quite a considerable strain on rail transportation. As the people in my constituency are affected, is the minister in a position to give us any information on whether the Canadian National Railway Company has any intention of completing this gap some time in the near future?

I thank the hon. member for Vegreville for his interest in the unfilled gap between Heinsburg, Alberta and Frenchman's Butte, Saskatchewan. The Canadian National Railways have been giving some careful study to this line, not only in 1949 but in 1948 and 1947; and, I must tell my hon. friend, they have it fairly high up in their priority list. But the Canadian National Railways follow a careful pattern and put branch line construction in two categories: those which the management feels it should recommend on the basis of improving or rounding out the system and serving territories without service, which lines can be economically justified; and those which can be regarded as colonization or development projects. With regard to the latter, they would probably look for government assistance if it was felt that a line was justified.
This line evidently would not fall in the latter category; it would fall in the first category. Until the Canadian National Railways can recommend to the government that it is a profitable line from the point of view of revenue operation and so on, I do not think I would be justified in bringing it down. But 1 can tell my hon. friend that the discovery 45781-79J

of the oil wells and the salt mines are two features which should add considerably to the chances of construction. They certainly should add to the economic advantages. The best I can say at this time is that the Canadian National Railways have the matter under careful review and that they have it fairly high up in their priority list.

I should like to bring to the attention of the minister some of the gaps in railway lines that exist in my constituency and in areas adjacent thereto. It seems to me that in the past a pattern was followed of building branch lines out from the cities of Moose Jaw, Weyburn, Estevan and the town of Assiniboia and not joining those branch lines in order to give the best possible service to the people in that area. With the branch lines existing as they do, the result is a long freight haul for livestock going to market, with shrinkage in weight, and possible loss in grade. For the farmers along these lines who have to use them for that purpose, it is an expensive method of shipping livestock. It means, too, varied and inefficient passenger service. For instance, going from the town of Valmarie to the city of Moose Jaw, only some hundred and seventy-five miles away, one must spend two nights on the way to Moose Jaw. The territory that I represent seems famous for having many gaps between various branch lines. I mention the gap between Neptune and Radville, a distance of some sixteen miles, and the gap between Willow Bunch and Assiniboia, a distance of thirty miles. The people in that area have been promised that the Canadian National railway line would be completed and extended. They have been promised that for many years. There is a town of St. Victor which exists beyond the railway line, and which has no railway service. That inland town sprang up there because the people of the district felt that the Canadian National railway line would be extended in the future. I might mention also the gap between Cardross and Dunkirk, a distance of nineteen miles, the gap between Neidpath and Swift Current, a distance of thirty miles. The tracks have been laid between Neidpath and Swift Current, but the line is still termed "under construction", and there is no train service between these two points. I might also mention the gap between Minton and Big Beaver. I had representations from people in that area asking the government to do what it could to see that that gap is bridged. I want to mention specifically and especially the gap between Mankota and Valmarie, and bring that to the attention of the minister.

Supply-Transport
A few years ago the Minister of Agriculture made the statement that it was his understanding that that gap would be bridged as soon as the Canadian Pacific Railway undertook branch line construction. In this house two years ago, the Minister of Transport himself said that that was his understanding; that that was one of the first programs for branch line construction of the Canadian Pacific Railway. It seems to me that the people in that territory have waited far too long for the bridging of that gap. I wonder whether the statement of the Minister of Agriculture will be fulfilled and that gap will be bridged.
Can the minister tell me whether or not the program will be undertaken at any time this year, ten years from now, or any time in the future to bridge that gap? The people in that area are getting pretty discouraged about the whole matter, and they would like some concrete undertaking, if possible, that that gap will be bridged.

I can tell my hon. friend immediately that if he understood a statement of mine made two years ago to mean that this gap would be bridged he is entirely mistaken. I do not think I would ever attempt to make a statement of that kind concerning the Canadian Pacific Railway. What I did tell my hon. friend-and I speak now of course only from memory; I have not seen the record-was this, that I would take the matter of the Mankota-Valmarie line up with the management of the Canadian Pacific Railway, although I made it quite clear to the committee that no jurisdiction lay with me in so far as that company was concerned. I did take it up with them and I presume I wrote my hon. friend along the lines of the reply that I received from the Canadian Pacific Railway, which I think was to the effect that at that time there was no intention of filling the gap because they felt their main task was to rehabilitate existing lines and purchase new equipment such as box cars, diesel engines and the like. I do not know on what basis the Canadian Pacific Railway proceeds, whether it follow the same course as the Canadian National Railways or not. The Canadian National Railways proceed along the line I mentioned a moment ago; if a line is economically justified it is likely to be placed on a list where the railway will sooner or later recommend it. If it is not considered to be a profitable undertaking from a straight operating standpoint but there is great pressure for it, I think the railway would then ask if the government is prepared to assist. These are the two bases. But dealing with the lines mentioned by my hon. friend, in so far as the Canadian

National Railways are concerned, the position is just as I related it to the hon. member for Yegreville.

If I might just make an observation in answer to the minister I would say that I am sorry-and I am not asking him to lay down the policy of the Canadian Pacific Railway-that he has to inform me that the Canadian Pacific Railway has no definite intention of building the line in the near future.
May I refer to Hansard of July 2, 1947, at page 4999 and read what the minister said:
I am informed by the officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway Company that just as soon as they begin branch line projects the Mankota-Valmarie line is one of those which will be considered.

That is not what my hon. friend said. My hon. friend said that I had made the statement. How could I possibly interpret the Canadian Pacific Railway policy? I could not. What I did was to pass on to my hon. friend the information that the officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway gave me. I did that only as a matter of courtesy to my hon. friend because I have nothing to do with the Canadian Pacific Railway. It is clear that in that statement I was passing along to him what the officers of the Canadian Pacific Railway had told me.

I accept the minister's explanation completely, and I did not mean to infer anything else. I am sorry that the Canadian Pacific Railway is not in a position to tell the people of the area that that gap will be bridged and that they will get efficient train service.

I rise to support hon. members who this afternoon have advocated a Canadian coastguard service. I am interested in the great lakes and in lake Ontario in particular. I might tell the minister, through you, sir, that so far as lake Ontario is concerned these facilities are available under another department. The only service that I know of at the moment is harbour patrols. I believe there is a harbour patrol in Hamilton and in Toronto, but these are only small vessels for lifesaving purposes. Under another department of the government we have stations at Hamilton, Toronto and possibly Kingston. There are ships and personnel available. With no great additional expense I believe that on lake Ontario at least we could have a coastguard service operated by the department of defence.

Mr. Chairman, this matter of a coastguard is of course of interest to many hon. members coming from the maritimes, the lake districts, and the west

coast. At the outset I want to say how much I was impressed by the words of the hon. member for Nanaimo. One of our biggest problems in this connection is the matter of co-ordination. If we could get several departments working in conjunction with one another in arranging this service we think that it could be much more economical than it is at the present time. I believe that it would give a much better service to those who are interested. I speak particularly now of the bay of Fundy district and of our fisheries and our lifesaving service. For quite some time the department has had under discussion the establishment of a lifesaving service on Grand Manan island. At the same time we must maintain a fisheries patrol boat there twelve months of the year. Although these men have busy times I believe there are many days when they can find little to do. But with two services and two crews the department is left open to criticism from many people. In fine weather there would be very little use for lifesaving equipment. At that time the same boat could do the fisheries patrol work. Then, in the stormy weather you would have two crews on one boat to take care of some very serious condition that might arise.
I believe that by combining the two services under the Department of Transport or under the Department of Fisheries we may expect much better results at a smaller cost. In his statement this afterinoon the hon. member for St. John's East has indicated that perhaps our fishermen in Canada were not treated as fairly in the matter of government services as are the fishermen in the United States. In the matter of a coastguard service that may be true, because I believe the coastguard service in the United States is better than ours.
However the hon. member has been here for only a short time. I believe if he would look over the situation carefully he would find that this government has done a great deal for the fishermen on both coasts. I would refer particularly to the breakwaters and wharves built on the Atlantic and Pacific coasts, and in the great lakes area. Today the cost of those wharves and breakwaters would maintain in Canada a lifesaving service second to none. If one travels down the coast of Maine or any of the other New England states he will travel hundreds of miles before he will find a breakwater built and maintained by the federal government of the United States. They just do not do that for their fishermen. On the other hand, down where I live I feel the department and the government have been more than good to our people in the matter of wharves and breakwaters. The government has been
Supply-Transport
generous, and you may be sure those services are appreciated by the fishermen who use them. In addition to that we have cold storage and other services, and I believe the government has tried to be helpful to the fishermen.
I have heard the matter of lighthouses discussed on both sides of the border, and have travelled on the waters both sides of the border. They may have better buoys and lighthouses in the New England states than we have in Canada. However I believe we have done a good job on the bay of Fundy and along our coast line. It is being improved as time goes on, and we hope it may be improved to an even greater extent.
I feel that several departments have tried to be helpful, and have done much for our fishermen. Then, reference is made to lifesaving equipment by the hon. member for St. John's East. When he says that such equipment is of great assistance I would support him. However, in many sections of the maritime provinces our boats are not equipped with radio-telephone facilities; and without that equipment lifesaving equipment may be available within five miles, and yet that fact not be known. Before the service can be made to work effectively or the way in which we would like to see it work, our fishing boats must be supplied with radiotelephone equipment, in order that they may get in touch with one another.
I should like to refer to something that happened in my county last fall. A young veteran of the last war had his arm caught in a lobster hoist. He did not have radio equipment on his boat, but within hailing distance there was a boat that did have radio-telephone. They wired to Grand Manan, and when he arrived at North Head breakwater a nurse and doctor were in attendance. The young man was unconscious at the time. Without the radio-telephone service there is no doubt he would not be here today. Since that time he has been appointed to the customs service, and is getting along well on Grand Manan island.
I believe that radio-telephone in all branches of the fishing industry is one of the greatest things that could be installed, and would be most useful in a time of disaster. I believe if we could combine the two crews in one boat it would be more economical than having two boats and two crews. This could be under the direction of the Department of Transport or the Department of Fisheries, and if we had this service we would go a long way toward assisting fishermen on both the Atlantic and Pacific coasts.

Mr. Chairman, I know there are a number of hon. members who wish t*

Supply-Transport
speak in this debate, and they may be assured that I shall not detain the committee long in what I have to say. I shall be objective in my remarks, and conclude them as quickly as possible.
All hon. members are sent here for a purpose, and I recognize this item as one of the greatest importance to the people who sent me here. From the number of members who have spoken in regard to it, I would judge that it is of considerable interest to many constituencies.
The hon. member for Vegreville has just touched upon the Heinsburg gap, and I have noticed that the minister has some difficulty in pronouncing the name of Frenchman's Butte. That is in my riding and this particular gap is of special interest to me. In view of the discussion which has taken place I believe the minister's answer has covered the situation fairly well, and anyone who is interested either in my constituency or anywhere else may read in Hansard the exchange between the minister and the hon. member for Vegreville.
It is still a gap.
As the hon. member for Moose Jaw has said, it is still a gap, and we are keenly interested in its completion.
He knows all about missing links.

As some hon. members have indicated, we are not asking for new lines- and I want that to be clearly understood. Contracts were let; and then between 1930 and 1935 the government of the late Viscount Bennett saw fit to give the contractor a sum of money to release the government from the obligation of continuing with this construction.
Meantime many people had gone into and settled in those parts of Canada, with the understanding that the line was under construction and that if they stayed there they would be able to get their produce to market. I was pleased to note that the minister said one of the points which would be considered was as to whether the line was economical to operate, and that under that classification possibly the Heinsburg gap would not be considered.
I suggest that in the line farther north between Barnes Crossing and St. Walburg we have a line which is economical for the simple reason that it also was to connect up with the C.P.R., which runs to Prince Albert, and from Meadow Lake through to Bonny-ville, and the C.P.R. were to have running rights on the C.N.R. when the C.N.R. was built. This would give the C.P.R. direct connection from Edmonton to Prince Albert.

An official of the C.P.R. who surveyed the economic possibilities of the line at that time, and was stationed in the town of Meadow Lake, gave voice to the idea that it was an economic proposition.
Just to give some idea of how far the economy has come since that time, I have here a letter from the president of the board of trade at Meadow Lake which I received this week. I believe in my maiden speech I made mention of the grain shipped out of Meadow Lake. Since then some hon. members have doubted whether that would be possible. The president fortifies my first remarks, to the effect that there have already been a million bushels of grain shipped out of the town of Meadow Lake up to the 15th of October this year, and that there will be over two million more shipped from that point. Part of this grain comes from the territory not served by the railway; and, as I mentioned before, a million dollars' worth of grass seed was also grown along that line last year.
At the time the economic survey was made the town of Meadow Lake, for instance, produced little grain at all, possibly 100,000 or 200,000 bushels at the outside. At the present time the president writes me that a whole trainload is going out of the town of Meadow Lake every day. The hon. member for Vegreville mentioned the Redwater oil fields as being along this line. The town of Meadow Lake alone uses some 3,000,000 gallons of gasoline in a year, and it is just one point on the line. There are many other towns. As a matter of fact, within my constituency there are some 20,000 people in the region adjacent to it who would ship their products thereon.
Therefore there is no doubt about the economic factor. The other consideration is the fact that the government at one time committed itself to construct the line. They built most of the grade and left a small gap. There is no steel on that part of the grade.
As a result of the action of the government at that time, people settled there, and in spite of the transportation difficulties are now out-producing any other part of Saskatchewan. It is necessarily very good land, and there is no doubt about the economic value. That is one point I want to bring to the attention of the minister. I am not going to ask him, as the hon. member for Vegreville did, when it will come about. I know that he will make proper representations to the Canadian National Railways. As I have said, the action of the C.P.R. hinges entirely on when the C.N.R. line is constructed because the C.P.R. have running rights over the C.N.R. line when it is built. As soon as the

C.N.R. line is constructed the C.P.R. will no doubt extend their lines from Meadow Lake to Bonnyville and then run over that line.
The official of the C.P.R. to whom I have referred made a survey of the economic possibilities of the land some years ago and said at that time that when the line was completed his company intended to run a daily train between Edmonton and Prince Albert each way. If it was economically possible at that time it is ten times more so now. I think I have taken up as much of the time of the house as is necessary to place the case of the people of that district before the minister.

Mr. Chairman, we have had a most interesting discussion this afternoon on the question, of a coastguard. I have nothing to add to it because the ground has been well covered, but I think the minister can be quite sure that there is great interest, in the coastal areas of Canada and also in the great lakes area, in the establishment of a coastguard service for Canada. I should like to suggest to him that he ask the standing committee on marine and fisheries to go into the question. That committee has to meet at this session in order to deal with the bill being brought in by the Minister of Fisheries, or at least we were told last night that was probably what w'ould be happening.
That is right.

I think the committee could perform useful work if it also gave consideration to the question of a coastguard. Practically every hon. member who has spoken today on the subject is a member of that particular committee. I do not believe it would be wise to let the matter drag along. I believe if the standing committee on marine and fisheries were to consider it there would be far more chance of getting something done at an early date than if we merely have a discussion now and drop the matter. That is particularly so because it is a job of co-ordination, a matter of getting different departments together. The interdepartmental committee which the minister mentioned has been considering the question for quite a long time.
No, it has not. It is just a recent appointment.

I have a press dispatch from Vancouver dated April 16, 1949. It reports that the minister's deputy, Mr. Lessard, and the chairman of the Canadian maritime commission, Mr. Clyne, met representatives of thirteen coastal organizations in Vancouver to discuss the possibility of a coastguard service for British Columbia. Apparently
Supply-Transport
Mr. Clyne is chairman of the interdepartmental committee. He said at that time that they were there to listen to arguments for a coastal search and rescue service, that they had an open mind, and that a committee had been set up to study requests for such a service made by persons and organizations on both coasts. Will the minister tell us whether there has been any report to him yet by the interdepartmental committee? Will he also say whether he has any objections to having the problem considered by the standing committee on marine and fisheries?

As to the first question, there has been no interim report. As I indicated a moment ago, the matter is under discussion by the committee. It is a tremendous problem and one which it is not easy to determine without consideration of many factors. The hon. member seems to think we are going to have a discussion and then drop the matter. Perhaps he could have said that last year but certainly not now when, following the debate of last year and for other reasons, it was decided to set up a committee. Therefore the matter is not being dropped; on the contrary it is being studied by that committee.
With reference to the second suggestion, I do not think that it would be proper, when one committee is already dealing with the matter, to submit it to another committee for consideration.
One would be a house committee and the other is an interdepartmental committee.

I know, but without having gone into it fully I would rather be inclined to await the report of the interdepartmental committee before submitting the question to a house committee.
