Mr. Chairman, I wish to take this opportunity to request the government to oppose, through a representative with the board of transport commissioners, the proposed rate increases suggested by the Bell Telephone Company, which, to my mind, do not seem reasonable. I believe it is the government's duty to so act, for not only shall we have to pay more for our own telephones, but the increase in rates will perforce be a charge upon federal, provincial and municipal governments, a charge which will have to be borne by each and every one of us through taxation. Consequently, I believe that we should do everything it is humanly possible to do in order to force the

Supply-Transport
Bell Telephone Company to show proof of the absolute necessity of this increase in rates before the request is granted.
In the spring of 1948, the Bell Telephone Company submitted a petition to parliament for an increase in its capitalization.
This application was granted only after a promise was made by Mr. Munnoch, K.C., the representative of the company before the standing committee on railways, canals and telegraphs, as you will see at page 15 of the committee report under date of May 11, 1948. This was a reply given to Mr. Campbell, a member of the committee, and it reads as follows:

A while ago, I asked a question
that went unanswered. What I wanted to know is this:	The company is going to spend $1,000,000 on
rights of way, $42,000,000 on land and buildings, $97,000,000 on the building of centrals, $95,000 on the building of stations, $86,000,000 on city lines, $26,000,000 on trunk lines and $15,000,000 on general equipment, which adds up to $362,000,000. Can you meet those expenses and still maintain your present rates?
Here is Mr. Munnoch's reply:
Mr. Chairman, if I may reply, I would say that the total amount of the capital we are requesting will not all be issued at one time. It will be issued from time to time, as required for new facilities of the kind mentioned by the hon. gentleman.
As new facilities develop, they will become productive, that is to say they will yield revenues. It is impossible to say what will happen to telephone rates, but I can say that at the present time the company has filed no application with the railway board for an increase in rates and has made no preparation for filing such an application. We have carried on through the war period, and by reason of economies and technological improvements in telephony, we have been able to maintain our present rate structure since it was established in 1926. Now, as to the future, as long as by economies and technological development we can maintain our rates, we intend to do so but if the economic conditions under which the company has to operate compel us to seek higher rates, then the company will seek them. Such, in so far as I can describe, is the situation at the present time.
As far as I am concerned, I never believed that promise made by the Bell Telephone Company and I voted against the second reading of the bill asking for that increased capitalization, as will be seen on page 3506 of Hansard, volume IV, 1948 session.
The foregoing statement by Munnoch calls for a very close scrutiny. If the Bell Telephone Company was able to maintain its rates without change from 1926 to 1948, what has happened between 1948 and 1949 for the company to decide suddenly to ask for increased rates? Has the company lost some of its efficiency? Has it stopped advancing in the way of technical progress? Have its operation costs increased more in one year, from 1948 to

1949, than in the previous twenty-two years, that is from 1926 to 1948? Has it ceased making profits?
No, Mr. Chairman, by its present attitude the company is turning its back on the Canadian people, as represented by one of its parliamentary committees. I believe the only answer we should give to that monopoly is to have the federal government socialize it and in my estimation, Mr. Speaker, if we want to destroy the forces of communism, we must give satisfaction to the people who pay for public services; that is the best means at our disposal.
You know as well as I do, Mr. Chairman, that the Bell Telephone Company purchases all the material, all the technical equipment it needs from the Northern Electric Company without calling tenders from any other company.
I submit that part of the so-called "operating expenses" are distributed to the Northern Electric Company, a subsidiary of the Bell Telephone Company, made up of a few shareholders of the latter company. The profits of the company are not disclosed; they dare not distribute the profits of the Bell Telephone Company to its shareholders. And that is why, last year, the company increased its capitalization in order to spread out over a larger number of shares the profits remaining after the leakage intentionally directed towards the Northern Electric Company. The intention behind all this is to be in a better position to ask for an increase in rates, the shareholders supposedly earning practically nothing. An attempt is being made to conceal from the public the actual dividends earned and even to prevent the public from benefiting from this company's profits. It is a social injustice about which I appeal to the members of this house and, through you, Mr. Speaker, to the country as a whole. Since 1927, the Bell Telephone Company has never divulged the slightest part of its profits to the public, and has never effected any important revision in its rates.
Once more, do we wish to prevent the increasing communist forces from invading our country? Let us give the man in the street, who wants to live and breathe freely in this sunny land of ours, the means of living here; and let us give the people of Canada public utilities genuinely concerned with the people's interests.

As I said in this house in 1938, I maintain that part of what is called "operating expenses" is distributed to a Bell Telephone Company subsidiary, the Northern Electric Company, which has only a few shareholders. Profits are concealed by the directors. They do not dare distribute them either to the Bell Telephone Company nor to its shareholders. These tactics serve to cloak the real dividends. In this way, the public cannot benefit from the profits accumulated by the company. It is a social injustice, and typical trust behaviour.
In its issue of December 29, 1936, Labor, a Washington publication, supplies interesting details concerning those reprehensible practices:
The federal communications commission has investigated the Bell Company and another manufacturing concern which is one of its subsidiaries, the Western Electric Company Incorporated. The investigators found that about $500 million of the Bell Company's value equipment is watered stock, sheer vater.
Cyrus G. Hill, the board's chief engineer, explained how the American Telephone and Telegraph made such tremendous profits. He stated:
The Bell Telephone Company buys 92 per cent of its equipment from Western Electric, thus preventing all competition and making it possible for Western Electric to charge whatever they want. The money simply passes from one of the Bell Telephone Company's coffers to another.
Reference is made in the same article to the instrument commonly known as the French phone.
Because of extra charges, the company has made an additional profit of $24 million. The extra charges were made on the grounds that these telephones entailed additional expenses for the company. This claim is unfounded, said Mr. Hill. Actually, the new telephone permits colossal economies, by doing away with manufacturing costs of wires and other expenses totalling more than $85 million.
That is the method used in the United States.
The part played there by the Western Electric Company Incorporated in relation to the American Telephone and Telegraph Company is the same as that played in this country by the Northern Electric Company in relation to the Bell Telephone Company of Canada.
I have here a document which clearly shows how the Northern Electric Company is controlled by the Bell Telephone Company. I have managed to obtain the list of shareholders of the Northern Electric Company. It is quite short. It shows that there are only two big shareholders: the Bell Telephone Company of Canada and the Western Electric Company Incorporated. The first holds a block of 456,640 shares and the second a

Mr. Speaker, I wish to stress the fact that no Northern Electric Company shares are available on the market. No one can buy them. They are all held by the people I have just mentioned.
On the other hand, I am not the only one to allege that the Bell Telephone Company has the absolute monopoly of a great public service. Here is a reply given in 1938 by the present Minister of Trade and Commerce, who was then minister of transport, as reported on page 935 of Hansard, volume I, 1938 session. I quote:
We must all recognize that the Bell Telephone dompany has a monopoly of a great public service in the districts in which it operates, and it is entirely sound government to provide that a public service monopoly shall be regulated as completely as possible.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: May I remind all hon. members that there has been a lengthy discussion on item 453. I think I have given all the necessary latitude to hon. members to discuss general matters. Several members have raised points which, perhaps, could have been more properly raised on specific items. If any progress is to be made, I would venture to suggest that this general discussion should not last much longer. I understand that a few more hon. members wish to take part in the discussion, but I would ask the co-operation of all the members to facilitate the early passing of this item. Then, we could carry on with a discussion of the other items.

I am not going to pursue the subject mentioned by the last speaker. The subject I am going to raise is not covered by any item in the estimates, so that the only time I can raise it is on the general item. I am bringing the matter forward now because I desire to secure a statement of policy from the minister on employment on public works projects falling within the jurisdiction of the Department of Transport.
The minister knows something about the question I am raising because I wrote to him about it early in the session. It has to do with employment at the Sydney airport, and it appears as though many men would be required on that work. There are many unemployed in the area. According to the telegrams and letters I have received from both individuals and organizations, anyone applying for employment at that airport is obliged to go to the two defeated candidates in the riding, one a druggist and the other a local magistrate, and secure from them a slip entitling the person to employment.
I should like to point out to the minister that the government maintains a chain of employment offices across this country known as national employment offices. In these offices there is a veterans' counsellor who is supposed to see that the veterans get preference in employment, particularly on public works projects. These offices have a list of all the unemployed in the community, and know the trades or vocations for which these people are fitted. The officers in these employment offices know the men who have been unemployed the longest, and generally try to give preference to the men with families.	*
[The Deputy Chairman.]
As a result of the sort of action I have brought to the minister's attention, men have left employment, secured a slip and taken a job on this construction project. If we are going to justify the maintenance of these national employment offices, then I think it should be the policy of the government to give employment through them. The minister, who has supervision over public works projects, should notify all concerned to that effect. I believe patronage is a throwback to the past. We are starting to build Canada as a nation. We are going to amend our own constitution, and I believe it is time that vicious system of patronage, which creates unrest and disunity in a community, was abolished. I should like the minister to tell me whether it is his policy to route employment on projects under his supervision through the employment offices.
I believe my hon. friend knows full well that that is not the policy of the department.

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: I believe it is the other way round.
What did I say?

speakerposition: Whip of the Co-operative Commonwealth Federation
speechtext: The member just asked if it was not the policy of your department to route employment through the national employment office and you have said, "No, it is not."

It is not the policy of the department to exercise patronage in connection with any of these jobs. I told my hon. friend, and I thought I had satisfied him, that the point did not arise on that project. Why? Because the contract for the work at the airport was given to an individual contractor. Once the contract is given out, I can tell the member immediately that neither I nor the officers of the department assume any control over the employment of men by the contractor; that is his responsibility. We exercise control over the work. I would be greatly surprised to learn that any of our officers had given instructions to the contractor.
As I indicated in my reply to the hon. member, if he can tell me of such a case I shall be glad to look into it immediately. In the instance mentioned, I do not see how the question could even arise since the contractor is the one who employs the men. The information I received concerning his method of procedure is to the effect that he secured his workers through the employment offices of that district. If my hon. friend shakes his head that that is not the case-
That is not the case.
Then, I have no authority in that regard because, once the contract is given out, the responsibility lies with the contractor.

I am not going to argue with the minister, but he is cutting corners. The minister let the contract. During the war there was a clause in those contracts outlining the basis upon which employment should be given. If use is not made of these employment offices for that purpose, they should not be there. Money is being wasted. If someone outside looks after employment, the veterans' counsellor is rendered impotent so far as doing the job he should be doing is concerned. The contract is let by the Department of Transport, and there should be some understanding as to the basis upon which employment is granted.
I am not asking favours. I am merely asking the minister to see that the facilities provided by the taxpayers' money are being used. I believe the project at Sydney will be fairly large, with a couple of million dollars being spent on it. The employment offices in that district are efficient, and I know they would do an excellent job if there were no interference. I know it is not the minister's policy, and I know no official of his department would issue those instructions. But it is the unwritten law that defeated candidates or members in a riding who represent the government have the patronage, and that old system goes on. It is outdated, however. You replaced it with your employment agencies, and I think it is time we started them to work. If it is not the policy now, I believe that in future, with regard to any contractor who is doing a public works project, there should be a clause in his contract to the effect that anyone employed on that particular job should, so far as possible, be obtained through the employment agencies. Those agencies have lists and all that kind of thing. While the minister assured me that it is not the policy of his department-and I believe him-at the same time he has now made a public statement to that effect and it goes across the country. That is why I asked him that question.

If it is good to attack the minister, it should also be good to say some good words in his behalf. I should like to say that there is no patronage in my part of the world. We have six big airports up there. We are spending millions of dollars. But I have not been consulted, nor have any of the members of my organization which, Mr. Chairman, is the Liberal organization in the district. I hope that you are not going to bar Liberals from working on these projects. I want to say that in the northwest country
Supply-Transport
there is not any patronage. That goes for my friends from the Yukon, the Cariboo country and along the northwest staging route where important work is being done. In fact, a little bit of patronage might help one out somewhat.

A few moments ago, Mr. Chairman, you said that we should not take too long on this item. A good many things have been said today. As to the coastguard, I must say that is a matter I spoke on here once before but it has been put away in mothballs, as someone said today, for safekeeping. I hope the minister will be in a position to look into the matter of the coastguard service on the Atlantic. I rise at this time, however, to speak on another matter. I had intended to do so earlier, but I could not get an opportunity inasmuch as I could not catch the eye of the Chairman, not being able to jump up as quickly as can some of the other hon. members.
I should like to have brought this matter to the attention of the committee at the beginning. It has to do with the item before us, item 453, and is with regard to the amount of money that is being spent in Transport. The total vote in the main estimates this year is $76,147,629. That is an increase from last year. I am glad to see the increase because in my constituency we hope to get an increase in the various subsidies, grants and so on and the work to be accomplished there. In addition to this $76 million, however, we have in the details a report giving us what the money is spent for, but it does not give us the details for the total amount. There is some $11,414,429 in the main estimates for which we have no details whatsoever. We do not know what it is being spent for, only under one name and one item.
Let us take, for instance, the item we are dealing with. There is an amount of $836,737 that we are voting on. On that item, we have details for $357,655. But we are voting the whole amount, and there is an amount of $381,632 as to which we have no details whatsoever. We are asked to vote the usual blank cheque for it. While it does not seem to be a great deal of money in these times, I think this committee should have some idea as to how this money is being spent or misspent. It is all under the one item called temporary assistance. On several occasions I have brought this matter to the attention of the committee. I believe the committee should have some idea as to where this money is going and how it is being spent. If it could not be done for the year that is being voted, we might have it for the past year.

in some departments-and possibly it is so in the Department of Transport-they are no more guilty with respect to these amounts they ask a blank cheque for than are others; the Department of Transport is no more guilty than all of the others. Yes.

Can the minister tell me whether or not any consideration has been given to the building of a spur line from Edmonton to Devon? Devon is right in the home of the Leduc oil fields. Contrary to the publicity given to the Redwater fields-
Is it Canadian National or Canadian Pacific territory?
Canadian Pacific.

I believe it is Canadian National, but I am not quite certain. The fact is that the town of Devon has absolutely no rail outlet. It is right in the middle of the Leduc field which is, contrary to some opinion, a great deal larger than the Redwater field. As a matter of fact the Leduc field contains 294 wells, as compared with 127 in the Redwater field, and produces 27,466 barrels of oil weekly as compared with 13,408 barrels from the Redwater field. The Redwater field does have an outlet to the Canadian National Railways running into Edmonton. Can the minister tell me whether or not anything has been done about this spur?

If it is Canadian National territory I am sorry to have to tell my hon. friend that I am not familiar with it. I am not aware that any consideration has been given to it. If it is in the territory of the Canadian Pacific Railway I would not be aware of it in any event, but I shall be glad to inquire and find out what the situation is.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 66, to incorporate Alberta Natural Gas Company.
He said: In moving second reading of this bill-
Louder.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
I shall get my voice in a moment. So far I have only said about four words of any importance, and they were not controversial. I shall speak a little louder from now on. In moving second reading of the bill, I would simply say that it is an incorporation similar to a number that have passed the house already. Following upon the discovery of so much oil and gas in Alberta, there were a number of combinations of persons who came before parliament to ask that
Alberta Natural Gas Company they be granted charters by way of special act in order to pipe oil and gas from Alberta to other parts of this continent. I believe in the second last session of parliament certain applicants came forward but were stopped until the government decided on a general policy. The general policy was decided upon, as many hon. members of the house will recall, toward the end of the last session of the last parliament.
A bill was passed, which we call the Pipe Lines Act, with a view to regulating the whole business course of any such companies, and in particular the route that any pipe line might take. Following upon the passage of that measure, as many hon. members of the house will recall, several companies were incorporated. There was one company-I do not know whether its name last session was the same as in the present bill, but I think it was-which failed to receive its charter at that time. I believe I would be correct in saying that it was because of the fear that it would route its line to certain parts of the United States. Whether or not I am right in that perhaps does not matter, but that is my recollection.
The same people are now seeking a charter. The bill before the house is either exactly the same as the other bills which resulted in charters to these various other applicants, or else it is so close to them that there is not very much difference. I have noted myself this evening for the first time in the powers set forth in the bill that the company is taking the power to route its lines anywhere within or without Canada, which is different from another bill I sponsored last session. Of course the fact that they are asking for such power, and that they might be given such power, by no means determines that any line will be taken outside Canada. The policy that parliament set forth in the Pipe Lines Act last year was that all such decisions as to routes and many other things were to be determined by the board of transport commissioners, which was given power to hear and decide upon all applications of that sort under the Pipe Lines Act.
Therefore this bill is merely an incorporation, and it does not imply that pipe lines will be built outside Canada. At the same time, I think it would be right for us to assume that in this case, so far as the transport of gas out of Alberta is concerned, a pipe line will probably be routed below the forty-ninth parallel if the board of transport commissioners agrees. At any rate, it is right that we should assume that, because certainly I do not wish to tell the house that it will not be so. I do not know whether or not it will be. The information that has been given to me is that five different pipe

Alberta Natural Gas Company lines have been surveyed, and I understand some of them are outside Canada. I suppose the facts will all be laid before the board of transport commissioners and it will determine where the route will go. Therefore it is just as well to assume that an application will be made to the board of transport commissioners to permit a line to be built outside Canada.
Did the hon. member say five lines have been surveyed; and by that does he mean surveyed in the engineering sense?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: Yes, five different routes have been considered and sufficient survey made of them that there are plans of all five to be placed before the transport board. That is what I intended to say.
If I may ask a supplementary question, are they to be placed before members of parliament, too?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext:
My information is that all these plans will be available to the committee of this house, so the answer to that question is yes.
My next comment is that in connection .vith pipe-line routes and everything else related to the transmission of gas or oil, in addition to the control of the transport board the province of Alberta is exercising control. That province, for instance, requires that gas shall not be taken out of the province until the needs of Alberta are met. The mere fact that a group of applicants are granted incorporation by this house does not mean that any gas can be taken out of Alberta without the consent of the government of that province. Indeed I am quite sure every hon. member knows that this parliament could not give any such right, in any event. Probably it is also well known by hon. members that Alberta is undertaking to exercise careful and strict control with respect to gas and oil.
There is one other control I think hon. members might keep in mind when considering any arguments that may be advanced in reference to gas being exported from the country. No gas can be taken out of the country except under permit granted by the Department of Trade and Commerce under the Electricity and Fluid Exportation Act. There can be no export of gas or electricity- electricity does not come into this question, but it happens to be in the title of the act- without permission of the Department of Trade and Commerce. Any permit of this kind given to a company is an annual permit, and renewal could be refused if there were any tapping of the line outside Canada, or anything like that. It would be a simple matter, of course, to turn the valve on the Canadian side and prevent any gas going
iMr .Maybank.]

across the line if there were any attempt to evade the conditions of the permit. One might look upon any pipe line going from the southern part of Alberta west across the United States to somewhere near the Pacific coast and then north into Canada again as transporting gas in bond through the United States. There would be an analogy to the transport of goods in bond.
That is practically all I have to say at this moment. This is a mere incorporation, such as we have granted many other people. The people seeking this incorporation will be in competition with many others to whom we have given the privilege of transporting oil and perhaps gas, and this bill involves nothing more than that. Those who are concerned with respect to the route this pipe line may take need have no more fear concerning this particular company than any of the other companies this parliament has already set up, and in addition there are the several controls I have mentioned. All the facts that I have not had time to mention-and indeed many that I would not even know-can be brought forward if second reading is given and the bill is referred to the appropriate committee. I do not urge the bill strongly upon the house, except in this way. When first one group and then another are granted the right to endeavour to persuade the transport board to permit them to construct pipe lines, it is hardly fair to refuse the same right to others in the same position. It seems to me that when reputable people come forward asking only that which has been given to others, and subject to proper controls, surely it is fair to give that group the same rights we have given others.
Would the hon. member name the companies he referred to, which have been granted incorporation to carry oil and gas to the west coast?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I did not say-
You said several companies.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I do not think I said any company had been granted the right to transport oil or gas to the west coast. Last year we incorporated a company called Western Pipe Lines and gave that company, subject to the approval of the transport board, the right to lay down lines anywhere in Canada, which would include the west coast.

I should like to correct the hon. member, because I do not think he wants to give a false impression. As far as I know the Westcoast Transmission Company Limited is the only company on the west coast.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I did not even know that company had been incorporated.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: I accept the apology, of course, but I really do not think it was necessary. speechtext: I thought they were given power to lay down pipe lines anywhere in Canada, subject to what the board of transport commissioners might say. Certainly that was the case with the company I mentioned a moment ago, Western Pipe Lines; that is what it says. I do not think they went west; I believe this is the company which is bringing oil from Alberta south of Winnipeg down to Duluth.
That is oil.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Assistant to the Minister of Mines and Resources
speechtext: Yes, not gas. I can see that the hon. member who has been so continually interrupting keenly desires to make a speech, and I feel that I shall be imposing upon him if I prevent him from doing so any longer. I do not want him to break the harness that so far has held him back; I have said practically all I wanted to say, so I yield my place to him.

Mr. Speaker, as the hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) has said, this same bill was before the house last year, at which time it did not come to a vote and did not pass; and I trust it will receive the same treatment on this occasion. I am opposed to the passage of this bill because it would grant a charter to this particular company to construct a pipe line which, in my opinion, would be prejudicial to the interests of Alberta, British Columbia, the city of Calgary and Canada as a whole. I propose to discuss this bill under those three general headings. Naturally, I am here representing the constituency of Calgary East which contains a large section of the central part of the city of Calgary. The interests of my constituents in Calgary must be one of my prime concerns. I believe that the construction of the pipe line proposed by this bill would be prejudicial to the interests of the people in Calgary East.
First, perhaps I had better say something about the source of supply which this company proposes to tap. I understand that the
Alberta Natural Gas Company main source of supply the company intends to use initially is a large gas field in the Pincher Creek area. Two very deep wells have been drilled there, and have disclosed the existence of a large gas field. As I remember, these wells are between eleven and twelve thousand feet deep, and each of them is rated as being capable of producing approximately 400 million cubic feet of gas per day. There is no doubt that there is a large amount of gas in the Pincher Creek area.
The proposed route runs from this Pincher Creek gas field through the Crowsnest pass and thence into the United States at Kings-gate. From there it goes down to Spokane and then west to a point between Seattle and Vancouver. The company proposes to supply the cities of Spokane, Seattle, Tacoma and Portland in the United States, with a branch line running to Vancouver, British Columbia. As was indicated by the sponsor of this bill, five routes have been surveyed by the company. The route they propose to construct is the cheapest one, and is the one I have indicated. One of the five alternative routes runs entirely in Canadian territory just north of the United States boundary. From all I have been able to learn about it, I doubt that it is a practicable route. The other three routes go through the United States for part of their length.
I should like now to say something about the general situation in Calgary so far as gas is concerned. As most hon. members probably know, the people of Calgary have done most of their heating and cooking for a long period of time by means of natural gas. There are a very few electric stoves. A good deal of the manufacturing industry in the province is based upon the use of natural gas for power and heating. Originally the source of supply of gas for Calgary was the Bow Island field between Lethbridge and Medicine Hat. That field was commencing to play out when the Turner valley gas and oil field came into existence as a big producer in 1926. For the past twenty years, our chief source of supply in Calgary and southern Alberta has been the Turner valley. It is now estimated that the Turner valley field will be exhausted within ten years.
In support of that proposition, I should like to read a statement made by the Hon. Mr. Maynard, the attorney general of Alberta, before a sitting of the board of transport commissioners held in Ottawa on September 21 and 22 in connection with an application by another company to export gas from this country. Mr. Maynard's statement reads in part as follows:
We are very much concerned with the situation in the south. The city of Calgary at the present time is supplied by the Turner valley and it is
1248	HOUSE OF
Alberta Natural Gas Company estimated that the gas reserves of Turner valley will be exhausted in approximately ten years. And if that is the case, then Calgary will have to be supplied by some other gas field.
There are two gas fields available in the south at the present time from which the city of Calgary could be supplied:	Jumping Pound field, a little
west of Calgary, and the Pincher Creek field in the southern part of the province.
We felt that the gas in the southern part of the province should be reserved to supply not only the city of Calgary, when the reserves of Turner valley are exhausted, but any other southern community, and should also be retained for the supply of other Canadian communities, such as Winnipeg and Regina, and so on.
That is the attitude taken by the attorney general of Alberta just a few weeks ago in connection with the piping of gas supplies in the Pincher Creek area to foreign sources.
I do not think there is any question that the building of the proposed pipe line to take gas from the Pincher Creek area will prejudice the long-term supply of the people in Calgary and southern Alberta. It is bound to shorten the length of time which people in that area will be able to make use of gas.
I think there is no question, either, that it will prejudice them so far as price is concerned. The projected consumers in the American cities and Vancouver will be prepared to pay more for the gas than is being paid now for it for industrial and domestic purposes in southern Alberta. The argument is advanced that the price paid by those people will be not only the price of the gas itself, but the cost of the transmission of that gas.
The advantages of gas, from the point of view of handiness, cleanness and so forth, are so great in comparison with solid fuels such as coal or fuel oil that there is no question but that the people on the Pacific coast would be prepared to pay considerably higher prices than those the people of Alberta have been accustomed to paying. For those reasons, I believe the construction of this proposed pipe line would be prejudicial to the best interests of Calgary and southern Alberta as a whole.
I should like to turn now to the case of Alberta and British Columbia generally. First, only a small part of the length of the proposed line would be in Alberta and British Columbia. In other words, it would serve a minimum number of people in those two provinces, as compared with other projected schemes. In my opinion, if a gas line is built through Alberta and British Columbia it should be one which would serve the maximum number of people in both provinces, rather than the minimum. The second consideration is that the whole Crowsnest pass area in Alberta and British Columbia is supported almost entirely by coal mining. The building of this gas line through that pass would adversely


affect the prosperity of that coal mining industry. From what I have been able to gather, the result would likely be the closing of about half the mines now in operation in that area owing to cutting off the markets. Another consideration is this. If this line were to be put through, as is proposed, once the line went outside Canada at Kingsgate it would pass out of our control as far as Canada is concerned and out of the control of Alberta or of British Columbia as far as the provinces are concerned. The line then going on into the United States is under United States control and gas which is going through it is under their control also. If there is any question of the failing of the gas supply, I do not think there is any doubt as to who first is going to get whatever gas is going through that line. It is all very well to say that the regulations put through by the board of transport commissioners, by the Alberta government, or by anyone else you will, are designed to ensure that Canadian needs will be served first. But once that gas has passed out of this country and is in the United States, if there is a matter of allocation of that gas as between United States cities which need it, and where there are people who are likely to be cold if they do not get it, and Canadian cities, I think one would need to be naive indeed to accept the suggestion that Canadian cities would get it. I do not think there is much question that the gas, once it is in the United States, would go to the United States cities.
The Americans kept us going in oil during the war.
And we kept them going in fish and lumber.

The hon. member for Winnipeg South Centre (Mr. Maybank) said that it would be a simple matter, as I think he expressed it, to turn the valve and stop this gas from going there. To begin with, it must be remembered that in this pipe line the valve would also be serving Vancouver; and if you turned the valve to prevent the gas from going to the United States, you would also be cutting off Vancouver from its supply. Therefore I do not think it would be so simple to turn the valve.
What would my hon. friend be doing for a shirt now if we did not get cotton from the United States?

I do not think that interjection by the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mitchell) has much to do with gas. As a matter of fact, I think the kind of gas that he is most familiar with is not the kind of gas that goes through a pipe line.
Nor is what I am listening to now.

Another consideration in that regard is this simple one. Where you are situated on a railroad, a road, a gas line, an oil line or anything else, it is much better for you to be near the start of it or along the route of it rather than to be at the end of it. If you are at the end of it, you are always likely to get the worst of the deal if there is any question of shortage difficulties or anything else along that line.
There is one other point I should like to mention in this regard, Mr. Speaker. As far as I can make out, only one gas line to the Pacific coast is a practical proposition at this time. Two of them could not operate profitably. There is not sufficient market. So it is probably going to come down to the point that a decision will have to be made some place, either here, by the board of transport commissioners, by the Alberta government or by somebody else, as to where this one line is going to run and who is going to build it. I am opposing this line because I should not even like to see it as a contender. I think that it would be so much worse than any of the other projected lines I have heard of that, as I say, I should be exceedingly happy if they had no charter and were not even contenders for securing the right to build a pipe line.
In that connection, may I say that a line through the United States such as is proposed would retard development in the northern part of British Columbia and in northern Alberta. On the other hand, a line running from the north central part of Alberta down through the north central part of British Columbia would have more influence than anything else I can think of in opening up a vast tract of country that at present is undeveloped. If the gas line to the coast and Vancouver were built along that route, it would mean the development of whole new large communities, in much the same manner as they have developed where oil fields have been discovered in Alberta during the past twenty years; for instance, in the Turner valley field, the Leduc field, the Redwater field, and so on. If on the other hand, a pipe line such as the one proposed by this company is built, you will have no development in that northern area. I have heard the argument put up that if gas is found in large quantities in northern Alberta and in northern British Columbia, it should be piped along through to Edmonton and put into the Alberta grid system which is proposed, and from there out to Pincher Creek and from there out to this other route to the Pacific coast. That sort of proposal would kill development in the north. It would take
Alberta Natural Gas Company away the incentive on the part of large num-'bers of oil companies to drill further wells in the northern part of British Columbia and in Alberta, for this reason. Once the possible market for about half the product which a man drilling a well may expect to produce- in other words, the gas-is removed from it, a great deal of the incentive to drill in that area is gone. In that respect gas is quite a different commodity from oil. No matter where you find oil, you can transport it to market by some means or other unless you are in an extraordinarily inaccessible location. You can take it out by barrels, trucks, tank cars or, if you have enough, you can build pipe lines. But as to gas, there is only one way of marketing it and that is through a pipe line. If the pipe line which is built-and I am quite convinced that one will be built, Mr. Speaker-is not through the central part or northern part of Alberta and British Columbia, it means that the development of a great deal of our north country is going to be held back for a great period of time.
I should like to say a word or two more in connection with the way in which the building of a pipe line through that northern area would stimulate development. In order to construct the pipe line, a good deal of road would have to be built. In order to keep it maintained, those roads would need to be kept open. You, Mr. Speaker, know the effect the building of a road has on the development of any area. It opens up the area; it enables people to get in and it enables them to get their products out to market.
Another important factor is this. Once a gas line is built, the cost of building an oil pipe line along the same route would be much less than it would be if it were put through initially or by itself. You would have the route developed. You would have your maintenance of roads and so forth. The whole thing could be done much cheaper. I think there is little question that large oil fields are going to be discovered in the northern part of Alberta and British Columbia. As a matter of fact, only two weeks ago a large well was brought into production at Normand-ville; that was an oil well with a considerable amount of gas in connection with it.
Normandville is just south of Peace River.

Yes. A gas line through the United States would make the cost of gas in Vancouver and in other southern British Columbia points greater than in the United States cities immediately to the south of them, for this simple reason. The prices people in Vancouver would pay would be the cost of the gas plus the cost of transmission. The further the gas is transmitted, of course, the

Alberta Natural Gas Company greater the cost will be; and with Vancouver on the end of the line, naturally it would pay more. On the other hand, a line through British Columbia entirely would have just the opposite effect. The people at the end of the line would be United States cities, and they would be the ones who would pay the higher price, with a relatively lower price in Vancouver and in the rest of British Columbia.
There are a few aspects of this matter which I should like to bring to the attention of this house, and which I think will affect the general national interest. The first is that the gas in southern Alberta is the most economic source of gas to transport to Regina, Winnipeg and other points east. Whether we shall eventually have sufficient gas reserves there to be able to supply Toronto, Montreal and other eastern cities nobody knows, but a number of people think so. In any event,
I think it has been established that that gas can be taken more cheaply from the southern part of Alberta than from the northern part. The distance is less; the terrain is easy. Therefore the gas reserves which we have in the southern part of Alberta should be retained in this country and not exported across the border.
Next, an all-Canadian line would enable a considerable number of new industries to be started in this country. I have been given to understand that if the way is cleared for a twenty-four or twenty-five inch gas line to be constructed entirely on Canadian territory it would give rise to a new mill in Canada for the production of sheet steel to make pipe, and it would also result in at least one plant, and possibly more, being put up in order to manufacture valves, pipe fittings, compressors and other machinery necessary for the construction of such a line. On the other hand, if a large part of the length of any gas line which would be constructed is run through the United States there would not be sufficient markets for the pipe and other things needed in Canada to justify the setting up of factories for its production. We shall continue to have to buy it from other sources.
That brings to my mind another important fact, namely, the United States dollar situation. If the line runs entirely through Canada and gas is delivered to the Pacific coast cities of the United States, they will pay a price which includes the entire cost of transmission in Canada; in other words, the money that they will pay will be paid to us and thus result in a considerably greater number of United States dollars coming into this country than would be the case if part of the line ran through the United States.
The construction of a line entirely in Canada would have an important effect on


employment and wages. There would not only be the increased amount of employment provided by the factories I have mentioned, but all of the wages paid out for the construction of this line would be paid in Canada, and not a major part of them in the United States. All of the wages for maintenance would be paid in this country instead of a large portion of them across the border.
From the point of view of employment and wages it is considerably to the advantage of this country to have the line run entirely through Canadian territory.
I shall mention one other point, Mr. Speaker, and then I shall conclude. If the whole line is in Canada, with the entire cost of the transport of gas paid in this country, you have to quite an extent an effect like that of a tariff. It would protect Canadian industry and Canadian wages. Let me cite an example to show what I mean. In Calgary we have a nitrogen plant which produces nitrogen products used in explosives during the war. At the present time it produces fertilizer. I am told that that plant uses more natural gas every day than all of the domestic users in the city of Calgary. In other words, it is the biggest industrial user of natural gas in Calgary and in southern Alberta. If the proposed pipe line crosses into the United States at Kingsgate it would be quite possible to construct there, not far across the United States border, a similar plant to make nitrogen fertilizer, and the fertilizer so made-they would pay approximately the same cost for gas as the Calgary plant does and the distance to transport it would be just about the same-could compete on advantageous terms so far as we are concerned in that market in the United States and in a lot of markets of the rest of the world. On the other hand, if you had a line running through Canada to Vancouver then down into the United States a nitrogen plant put up there would have added on 10 cents, 15 cents, or 20 cents extra per thousand feet of gas for transmission costs. As a result of course the Canadian plant would have that much advantage in the world markets.
For all these reasons, Mr. Speaker, I think that in the interest of Canada as a whole, and in the interest of Alberta and British Columbia, and particularly the people of southern Alberta, this bill should be voted down.

Mr. Speaker, of all the addresses that I have listened to since coming to parliament the address by the hon. member for Calgary East (Mr. Harkness) is without question the most laborious. When I recall what has been

said by Alberta members in this house and by the provincial administration of Alberta itself, it seems to me that if the hon. member for Calgary East were to return to Calgary tonight in all probability they would fry him in oil because he is underselling the great potentialities of Alberta. In fact he has well nigh admitted that they have not gas. As a matter of fact it is a very good job that people who are interested sufficiently in bringing a gas line from Alberta to the Pacific coast are not here tonight to listen to the hon. member for Calgary East because I am sure if they were they would not invest a nickel in the project.
I am from British Columbia and I want to say that I, as one British Columbian, would be tickled to death to have gas piped from Alberta to the constituency that I have the honour to represent in this house. It is all very well for those in Calgary and Edmonton, who are enjoying the comforts of very cheap fuel, to sit back and talk about the potentialities fifteen or twenty years from now in the province of British Columbia when we may or may not have gas coming from that area into the great city of Vancouver.
I am supporting this bill because there are about twelve very simple reasons why I should do so, and I am going to enumerate them in the short time that is at my disposal. I am intensely interested in the prospect of having natural gas made available to the thousands of consumers in Vancouver. I am particularly interested that such natural gas be available to these consumers at the cheapest possible rate. It would appear that the only immediate prospect of obtaining such natural gas is from Alberta, despite the remarks of the hon. member for Calgary East.
Mr. Speaker, on a question of privilege-
The cheapest route over which to build and maintain-
Order.

On a question of privilege, I should like to point out to the hon. member, who apparently did not hear my speech, that I made no argument whatever against exporting gas to British Columbia-none whatever. It is the Canadian route about which I argued.

We will come to that. The cheapest route over which to build and maintain a pipe line from Alberta to the lower mainland of British Columbia is naturally over that part of the rugged Rockies which is the most suitable terrain-and the Rockies are not going to be moved tomorrow.
If part of that route should prove to be through the United States I, as a native-born Canadian, do not think that the price of gas in my constituency should be higher in order
Alberta Natural Gas Company to follow a more costly route, though that route might be through only the Dominion of Canada.
I am satisfied that the Alberta government and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Howe), in whose hands the export of gas rests, will impose suitable restrictions if the line goes through the United States, to ensure that the consumers on the Canadian Pacific coast will be served first, and consumers, for that matter, in the interior of British Columbia, who can be reached from the line, such as in the area of Trail, and the great Consolidated Mining and Smelting Company.
I am in favour of this company or any other bona fide pipe line company receiving a charter from this government. I understand this bill, as stated by the mover, is identical as to form with other pipe line bills, and has been approved as such by law officers of the crown. Whichever company succeeds first and provides cheap gas to British Columbia is, so far as I am concerned, completely and entirely satisfactory; and I hold no brief for any company in any particular sphere thereof. I do not think that any company composed of responsible people should be refused a charter by the government, thus creating a monopoly or monopolies for the company or companies already incorporated and who may or may not perform after the incorporation has gone through.
I am therefore, Mr. Speaker, heartily in favour of this government's granting the present charter.

Mr. Speaker, I believe there are a good many points that have been overlooked in this debate. This evening I shall not say too much either pro or con, although it was my opinion that an all-Canadian route would definitely be preferable.
I have in my hand telegrams passed between the Hon. Gray Turgeon and the premier of Alberta, which I should like to place on Hansard. This is the telegram from the Hon. Mr. Turgeon to Mr. Manning:
I should be glad to have answers to following questions as sponsor of the Alberta Natural Gas Company bill asking for charter enabling company to apply to board of transport commissioners also the government of Alberta and the government of Canada for authority to export gas from Alberta to Vancouver, British Columbia, and other parts of Canada, and to the United States.
Question No. 1. Is the government of Alberta opposed to the incorporation by the parliament of Canada under provisions of the Pipe Lines Act of the Alberta Natural Gas Company or any other bona fide company seeking power to build a pipe line under the Pipe Lines Act? The answer to this question would be based on the assumption that the ultimate intention of such company after receiving due federal and provincial authorization is to supply natural gas from Alberta to consumers in British Columbia and any surplus supply would go to consumers in the United States Pacific northwest.

Fish Inspection Act
Question No. 2. Has the Alberta government decided to prohibit the export of natural gas from any particular areas or sections of the province of Alberta?
Question No. 3. What is the general policy of your government in regard to export of gas from Alberta? I would greatly appreciate receiving reply today, Monday.
In his reply Mr. Manning had this to say:
Replying your telegram October 17, the following are the answers to the questions as enumerated in your wire.
Answer to question No. 1:	The Alberta government is not opposed to the incorporation of the Alberta Natural Gas Company or any other bona fide company under provisions of Pipe Lines Act but on the contrary feels very strongly that no bona fide company should be refused incorporation in that refusal would deprive the province of its right to deal with any or all legitimate companies interested in exporting gas and would restrict such dealings to those particular companies favoured by parliament for incorporation.
Answer to question No. 2: The Alberta government has not decided to prohibit the export of gas from any particular area of the province but has announced that it will not approve the export of any gas until fully satisfied that there are sufficient available reserves to meet the present and future domestic and industrial requirements of Alberta. The discovery of new reserves and/or integration of present fields could completely change the prevailing situation in any particular area.
Answer to question No. 3. The policy of the Alberta government respecting the export of natural gas is three-fold: First, to prohibit any export until fully satisfied that there are sufficient available reserves to meet Alberta's present and future domestic and industrial requirements; second, when satisfied that surplus exists over and above these requirements sufficient to justify export under sound conservation and proration practices the government will approve the export of such surplus with each application being considered on its own merits and in the light of all prevailing factors.
Third-
And I would call the attention of hon. members to this particularly-
It will be a condition of any export permit that Canadian requirements must be given first priority.
It being nine o'clock the house will resume the business interrupted at six o'clock.

speakeroldname: Hon. R. W. Mayhew (Minister of Fisheries) moved
subsubtopic: MARINE PLANTS- EXPORT AND IMPORT REGULATIONS
speechtext:
the second reading of Bill No. 63, respecting the inspection of fish and marine plants.
He said: Mr. Speaker, on October 13,1 made a brief statement on the occasion of the first reading of the bill. I shall make a further statement this evening explaining its purposes. May I say at the outset that it is our purpose to have the bill go to the committee on marine and fisheries where I am sure it 
will receive proper consideration and give all interested persons, both those in the house and those outside the house, an opportunity to discuss it. We have no control, of course, as to when the committee will hold its sittings, but we would hope that it would not convene too soon so that people from the outside sections of Canada might have an opportunity to attend, if they desire to do so.
At the present time the inspection of fish is authorized by two acts of parliament, namely the Meat and Canned Foods Act and the Fish Inspection Act, the latter covering fish other than canned. It is the latter act that now requires revision.
On moving second reading of the bill I should like to outline to the house the reasons for the revision, and the general principles of the bill. Two very important reasons exist to make revision necessary and desirable. On the one side is the need to help the further progress of the fishing industry itself. On the other is the legal weakness in the present act. A few words of explanation as to each of these are called for.
Some parts of our fishing industry have been asking for increased inspection services from the federal government. Within the industry, and particularly in its national organization, the fisheries council of Canada, there have been continuous discussions now for several years on the problems of the quality of product as it reaches the consumer. In canned fish, distribution and good quality are relatively easy problems to overcome. But in other types, fresh, frozen and cured fish, the main markets are far from the sea, and the product is very perishable. The industry has nevertheless increased its sales of these types, but the progress has been slow, and it has given serious attention to ways and means of guaranteeing quality to the consumer. In September, at a national meeting of the industry in Ottawa, a set of proposals was presented to the government aimed at a fuller development of the fisheries potential. Among others, the industry recommended that the government take certain steps to ensure proper handling of products.
The present bill is one instrument for aiding the development of good quality products. It is, however, only one, and other complementary steps are equally necessary. This country has already had much experience in agriculture as to methods of quality improvement. In many other perishable commodities, such as dairy products, livestock, fruits and vegetables, quality has greatly improved in the past two or three decades as the Department of Agriculture developed technical services for the farmer and instituted systems of inspection. The present bill before the house contains nothing

revolutionary. All its provisions are already in effect for other food products, and are to be found in existing acts of parliament, such as the Live Stock and Live Stock Products Act, the Dairy Industry Act, and the Fruit, Vegetables and Honey Act. The present bill asks the house to do for fisheries what has already been done for agriculture in the matter of inspection.
I mentioned before that inspection alone is not sufficient. There is a good deal of educational and demonstration work necessary among fishermen and processors and handlers of fish in certain regions. Such work always has to precede the institution of inspection. The Department of Fisheries today has inspection operating for products such as canned salmon and lobsters, salted and pickled fish, oysters, smelts and some others. For other types it offers voluntary inspection to the industry. Almost universally, however, courses of instruction, field interviews, and circulars have preceded the introduction of inspection. Usually also there has been a period of voluntary inspection preceding the compulsory. Today inspection regulations are screened through the industry before being made effective.
I mention these matters to emphasize two points, that education and demonstration work has to precede inspection, and secondly, that the fishing industry is consulted in the preliminary stages of consideration of any regulations to be made under the present act. I should like the house to note that particularly, because it is not the act itself as much as the regulations under the act that will affect the industry. We have promised the industry that we will discuss with them the regulations to be imposed under the act before they go into effect.
The existing act, which the bill under consideration would replace, has been on the statute books since 1914. It was first passed in order to improve the quality of pickled herring on the east coast. Under the authority of the existing act regulations have been made from time to time, and today regulations are in effect in respect of several varieties of pickled and salted fish, oysters and scallops produced on the east coast. The act has also been applied, and regulations thereunder have been made, in respect of white-fish which constitutes the principal commercial fishery in the three prairie provinces. It has not been applied to British Columbia, where inspection of canned fish alone takes place under the Meat and Canned Foods Act.
The authority of the parliament of Canada to legislate on this subject is derived from several heads of section 91 of the British North America Act, 1867, but principally from head 2, the regulation of trade and
Fish Inspection Act
commerce. Because the provisions of the existing act were not confined to export and interprovincial trade, some doubt arose as to the constitutional validity of the act. An expedient was adopted in 1932, and carried through to the present time, that when the act was to be applied to certain provinces they would enact enabling legislation, so-called legislation by adoption, whereby the provincial legislatures validated those parts of the act that might be within provincial legislative jurisdiction. This type of enabling legislation has been used for some of the acts dealing with agricultural products, and was also adopted for the Fish Inspection Act.
This type of enabling legislation has been successfully challenged in some of the provincial courts, and as a result most of the federal acts dealing with agricultural products were revised, and quality control statutes enacted by the parliament of Canada in respect of agricultural products are restricted more or less to export and interprovincial trade.
The present bill seeks to do the same thing for quality control of fisheries products. Prior to the introduction of the bill, informal discussions took place between officials of the Department of Fisheries and the provincial fisheries departments or divisions for the purpose of co-ordinating the federal and provincial legislation on quality control of fisheries products, and making the necessary administrative arrangements so as to be able to carry out the inspection program, not only at producer but also at wholesale and retail levels.
These discussions were held prior to the entry of Newfoundland into confederation, and included every province except Newfoundland. The Fish Inspection Act is one of those acts whose application to Newfoundland has been deferred. Under the confederation arrangements, consultations with the appropriate Newfoundland authorities are to be held before the act is applied in that province.
The bill will not become law immediately on royal assent, but will be brought into effect only on proclamation of the governor general in council. This will serve the purpose of timing the application of the revised act in order to co-ordinate it with any similar provincial legislation that might be enacted to cover sale and inspection within the province.
Before the introduction of the bill the fisheries council of Canada, representing the fishing industry, was consulted at its annual meeting in Ottawa in March of this year. The general view of the industry expressed by the council was to the effect that the government should have the necessary authority of parliament for any regulatory measures designed to improve the quality of fisheries products. The

Fish Inspection Act
industry, however, is more concerned with the type of regulatory measures that may be proposed from time to time. In practice, no regulation affecting any particular section of the industry is made until the opinion of such industry has been obtained and carefully considered. The Department of Fisheries is conscious of the fact that it is only by complete co-operation of industry and government that the problems of the quality of fisheries products will be solved.
If I may just add one word, personally I think nothing is more needed in our fisheries today than the assurance of high quality fisheries products when they reach the table; and I feel sure this can be achieved with the refrigeration facilities at our disposal. It is our desire and determination that this shall be carried out, in co-operation with those engaged in the industry as well as the provincial governments.

Mr. Speaker, I represent a constituency on Vancouver island adjacent to the constituency of Victoria, which is represented by the minister; and it affords me the greatest pleasure to be able to extend congratulations to him on this occasion, when he is introducing a measure in this house for the first time as a minister of the crown. This is a particularly happy occasion because as far as I know the legislation he is introducing is generally acceptable to the fishing industry, and that applies to the packing companies, the co-operatives, the small fishing concerns and the fishermen themselves. All these organizations are anxious to see the great industry of fishing put on a firm basis, improved in efficiency and made comparable with the other industries to which the minister referred, such as agriculture. If there is any criticism of this bill it may be that it should have been brought in earlier, but the minister did not have an opportunity to do so. So again I want to extend my congratulations to him on taking the first opportunity, since be became minister, to introduce this legislation.
As I said, I believe the general principles of the bill will be acceptable to the industry in all parts of Canada. The minister has said that this legislation will be referred to the standing committee on fisheries, whose members will have an opportunity to go through it section by section. I have only glanced through it, but with great surprise I noticed reference to the grading of fish. I am sure the minister realizes that as far as British Columbia salmon is concerned there is only one grade, and that grade is superb. I have frequently seen you, Mr. Speaker, partaking of meals in the parliamentary restaurant. There at times you have been able to enjoy
[Mr. Mayhew.l
the deep red-blooded spring salmon from British Columbia. At other times I have seen your face fall when you have been presented with colourless, anaemic looking fish coming from other parts of this country. Then I noticed that reference is made to supervision over the management of boats. I know the prowess of the minister in sailing small boats, because he comes very close to my home and goes fishing in Brentwood bay. There he manages his own boat, so I think he will appreciate that there is danger in suggesting too much management from Ottawa of boats which may be operated on either the Atlantic or the Pacific.
These are matters which perhaps can be better dealt with in committee, unless the minister cares to assure us that he does not question the excellence of our British Columbia fish, or the ability of our fishermen to handle their own boats.

speechtext: Coming from Nova Scotia, one of the great fishing provinces of Canada, I am naturally interested in this legislation. I assure the minister that because of my high regard for him I would be inclined to support the bill just because he has introduced it, unless it is shown to contain some weakness. I was pleased to hear my colleague the hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) say that all the fish coming from the Pacific coast are superb; but if it were possible to make a test in the parliamentary restaurant as between the superb fish coming from British Columbia and fish from the maritime provinces, especially the salmon, while the British Columbia fish would still be recognized as superb, I am sure the maritime fish would be even more superb. I am quite sure no one about to enjoy a fish meal in the restaurant-and there are not many of them -would fail to ask for maritime province fish as his first choice.

There are the British Columbia fishing interests, the great Nova Scotia fishing interests and we now have perhaps the even greater Newfoundland fishing interests. In fact every part of Canada is interested in commercial fishing to some extent. The minister has pointed out that, in this country, we desire well-graded fish of the highest quality. The Canadian population should be encouraged and educated to use more fish than in the past. The fishing industry has been the forgotten industry in Canada, but it is being recognized more and more as the years go by. There is a great deal yet to be done.

l believe the province of Nova Scotia has been more instrumental in advancing the interests of the fishing industry than any other section of Canada. It was through the efforts of the province of Nova Scotia, approved by the Ottawa government, that the commission headed by Sir Andrew Rae Duncan was appointed. This commission recognized that the fishing industry had been neglected and recommended that a special fisheries department under a separate minister be established. For many years the portfolio of that department has been tossed about from one person to another. I am glad that, at least as long as this government is in office, the responsibility of this ministry will rest upon the shoulders of my good friend the present Minister of Fisheries.
I have had some communications with respect to this legislation, one of which was from the fish packers association of the maritime provinces. This association has given study to the proposed legislation. They have some objections to certain provisions in the bill and have certain additions to propose. If this bill is referred to the special committee, as the minister indicated, that organization will have an opportunity of making representations and I am quite sure will be given full consideration.
In the maritime provinces there is an organization called the united maritime fishermen's association. That association has just held its annual meeting in my home town, Amherst. No doubt, as usual, they invited the Minister of Fisheries to attend. The objectives of the fishermen of this association are to secure quality products, fair prices, cold storage and refrigeration storage facilities, and the education of the consumers so that they will relish and use a greater quantity of fish than in the past. These men have been engaged in what was the forgotten industry of Canada.
I have seen on the wharves in Nova Scotia the fishermen come in with their boats loaded with fish. At times, the prices they were able to secure were as low as fifty cents a hundred pounds. Those days are gone, I hope forever. Even under those conditions, the fishing industry has been able to survive in my province. On behalf of Nova Scotia, I give this legislation my support, subject to its being referred to the special committee for improvement to meet the requirements of the fishermen, the processors and the consumers.

As another of the Nova Scotia members, I too am interested in the fishing industry and in any measure brought up in this house or any other house which I feel would be of some benefit to that industry. I certainly wish to give it my wholehearted support. May I say that I should have liked to see more members present tonight, in order that I could bring to the attention of so many of those who have spoken earlier on the subject of agriculture the fact that we in the east have a subject of interest. We have supported any measure we felt would help the west or any other agricultural part of Canada, and I should like to see more members present tonight so that I could plead with them for the support of the fishing industry, which is of particular interest to the easterner. I feel that the support we have given them, and are going to give them at all times, should be given to us in turn, when measures for our assistance are brought before this house.
The hon. member for Cumberland mentioned the low prices which our fishermen have received for their products. Of course, that was true, but I hope those times have gone forever. Our fishermen have not suffered from drought as the western farmer has, but they have suffered from drying up of markets. In this business which we share with our Newfoundland friends, there have been times when, after a season's arduous fishing, our people have found themselves in debt to the provisioner and supplier. The vessels would come into port with what was known in those days as a "broker"-owing to the condition of the market the vessel did not pay expenses.
I believe anyone who knows our Nova Scotia fishermen knows that they are enterprising and versatile. Through the use of their natural skills, they managed to earn a few dollars in other fields.
