speechtext:
I am not
talking politics, as I would remind the hon. member, but I do want to cover a few more points before I turn to the essence of the bill itself. I want to say first that until recent years those engaged in the business of buying and marketing fish were for the most part men who had learned the fish business "the hard way", having eventually graduated from the dory to the office desk. Cold storages, large and small, have been built all along our coast and today the fresh fish industry is of the utmost importance.
Those in the fish business realize without being told that good markets for their fish depend to a great extent on the quality. There has been little tendency to try to market poor fish, and I believe in general that regulations in respect of inspection of fresh fish as well as salt fish, as indicated in this bill now before us, will be welcomed by all. As an indication of this fact, and also for the sake of the information contained in them, I should like to read some excerpts from these letters. The first one I want to read is from the manager of one of the smaller plants down on our shore. He says in part:
In noting the content of this bill, it appears to be leading in the right direction. We believe the inspection of fish as has been carried on in recent years, particularly of canned lobsters and pickled herring, mackerel, etc., in containers, has brought beneficial results to all parties concerned, and with the inspection improved and extended we would hope for increased sales and more satisfied consumers.
It is not clear to me whether the act requires an inspection certificate to accompany every shipment of fish or marine plant, leaving the shipper's establishment. If it does, we fear that would cause delay in shipments, unless there is an inspector stationed at every shipping plant, as fresh fish shipments are mostly what we call rush shipments, to catch the first train or other means of transportation, so the products will arrive at destination as quickly as possible, which means better state of preservation. If at any point the inspector causes delay in transit of fresh fish for inspection purposes, the act will defeat what it proposes to aid.
I do not doubt for a moment that that is a live subject in the minds of the minister and

the officials of his department, but it is an important point; and I expect that points brought out by means of letters such as this will be cleared up.
Then I should like to read a small part of another one; it is from a plant which is a little bit larger than the one whose letter I have just quoted. The writer says in part:
In our minds there is only one method of inspection. It should start in the boats, from there to the fishermen. If they do not take proper care of their fish, they are of an inferior quality when they reach the wharf. The next inspection should start on the wharf and carry it through the plant and the processing of the fish-from the time they are taken in the plant to the time they are either shipped out or placed in the freezer. This is also my belief-fresh fish should be by express-no freight shipments. It would also be necessary to have inspection of the fish on arrival at the wholesaler's and from the wholesaler to the retailer, which means it is necessary, in order to obtain a good quality of fish, to have an inspection from the time the fish is caught until it reaches the consumer. This I believe is one of the impossible things to do as it would require a large number of inspectors, also very heavy expenses. We would think that one of the most important inspections would be from the retailer to the consumer as the producer is well aware if he ships out poor quality he is going to receive complaints and his business is going to suffer.
He winds up the paragraph with one little note that strikes a nostalgic chord in my soul. He says:
"I am not going to talk any more on fish as I have to smell it every day."
That particular smell of fish from the plants down our way is not the least bit unpleasant because the plants are all clean and their fish smells good. I like the smell.
To go a little further, I have the same document as the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) had. I think it should be pointed out to hon. members here that this association of fish packers of the maritime provinces:
... is on record with the department for several years recommending the inspection of fresh, frozen and smoked fish and has asked that inspection commence at (or before) the fish are landed, continuing throughout handling and processing and ending only when the fish are packed ready for transportation. This would guarantee that the fish were in good condition when landed, that they were handled and processed in a sanitary plant where proper sanitation and hygienic requirements as to plant equipment and personnel are observed throughout the entire process.
Having read those excerpts, I hope there will be no doubt in the minds of hon. members that this bill is really welcomed down our way.
I should like to say just a word about the inspectors. Before this bill is passed, I hope some amendments will be brought about by the committee, because there are some clauses in the bill which I and some others in the house do not agree should be put in it

at this time. I believe that really serious thought should be given to the matter of appointing qualified inspectors. Fishermen find it difficult to believe that a young man, just out of school, can learn to judge the qualities of fish merely by attending a short course provided by the Department of Fisheries. Wherever possible, appointments should be made not so much on scholastic standing as on the experience an applicant has had in the fishing industry.
It is our good fortune in Queens-Shelburne to have on the job now some inspectors who combine high educational standards with practical experience. I am informed by those who should know that the best inspector of pickled fish in Nova Scotia is one who would have a difficult time qualifying by educational standards alone. I suggest that there is an important place for those with high educational standards, who are to be engaged in office and administrative work in the department. But I also suggest that the men in the field who are to be given the power to approve or disapprove of the quality of fish for export to other provinces and countries should be appointed with the preference given to those with practical experience and knowledge.
Now I want to say just a few words about the latter part of the bill. As will be noticed, it relates to the inspection of fish and marine plants. Some of our inland friends may not even know what we mean by a marine plant. I should like to say that I am glad the bill recognizes the importance of marine plants by including them in the regulations. To many hon. members who may not know it, may I point out that the gathering and processing of Irish moss and kelp is an industry of some significance on our coast, and it is also an industry which has great possibilities for the future. In Clarke's Harbour, Shelburne county, there is a factory which buys kelp and processes it for export to Rockland, Maine, where finally various drugs and compounds are derived from it and they are sold all over the United States. The local manager of that plant told me last summer that, in the few years it has been running, upwards of $400,000 had been paid out in wages to the gatherers of kelp and to those who work in the plant preparing the kelp for shipment. That amount may not seem large, but I want to assure hon. members that it is a considerable amount when it is distributed in that small community of Clarke's Harbour.
I think this kelp industry is one that has great possibilities. It is hoped that the day will soon come when the derivatives can be extracted, packaged and exported from this little Nova Scotia community as well as from others, and I understand that some thought 45781-801
Fish Inspection Act
is now being given to that industry. I am informed that the particular growth of kelp on this coast contains a very high proportion of the substance required for the market, a much higher proportion than the growth along the coast of Maine; this fact accounts for the export of our kelp to that state. It is hoped that the research and marketing services of the Department of Fisheries will be directed toward an inquiry into the possibilities of this kelp industry. It might be proper for the biological division to investigate the methods of gathering kelp. It may be that seasonal restrictions will be found necessary in order that the plants will not be cut during their reproductive stage.
The gathering of Irish moss is an industry which likewise has great possibilities. It is a growing business down our way. In Shelburne there is a plant which processes it. In my home town of Liverpool the Best Yeast Company just recently put in a little side plant in which they are making this Irish moss into a delicious gelatine dessert. That is just a sample of what can be developed from Irish moss alone. What I have said about the part that could be played by the fisheries department in connection with kelp is of course also true of Irish moss. It is proper that this bill should contain some provision for the inspection of marine plants. Like the inspectors for fisheries, I really hope that the inspectors who will be appointed will know their job and will do it effectively.
Before closing my remarks I would reemphasize the need of carefully examining the qualifications of the candidates for inspectorships with regard to their practical experience and knowledge, and that preference be given those who possess these qualities. I am convinced that by so doing we can expect a much happier acceptance of these new regulations by the fishing industry, and that the purpose of the bill will be better served.

As a
member also who represents a fishing riding, in this case a west coast riding, I, too, would like to say a few words and to congratulate the minister, not only as Minister of Fisheries but also as the minister from British Columbia as well, on the introduction of this bill. The fishing industry in British Columbia has for many years realized the importance of insisting on a high quality for their products and, long before the government actually entered the field of grading and inspection, they themselves had in the industry an arrangement to grade and standardize their products.
The hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) mentioned quite rightly that our fish is superb. It is superb at the time it is

Fish Inspection Act
caught, but a lot can happen to fish between the time it is caught and the time it arrives in the housewife's kitchen. I think all members appreciate that when fish is caught it is very good, but when fish is stale it is very offensive. One of the reasons why the housewives of Canada have not used as much fish as perhaps they would want to is that occasionally they do get bad fish. That is one reason why I think the fishing industry on the west coast, which has always insisted on quality, will welcome this bill, because the government can do what industry cannot do. The government can see that everyone lives up to the standards which are set in this bill.
It is noteworthy too, I think, that it is the industry itself, not just the west coast industry but all the industry in Canada, which has asked for this bill. Some years ago there seemed to be a conflict between the fishing industries on the west coast and on the east coast. They found, as most people do find, that conflict is not of much value, and some years ago they got together and formed this very active body known as the fisheries council of Canada. This recommendation which is made by the fisheries council of Canada is an indication that west coast fishermen and the east coast fishermen can work together for the mutual benefit of the entire fishing industry.
There is one thing which I should like to mention in regard to the minister's speech, which has been commented on very favourably, but there was one thing which the minister's speech lacked. He was too modest to mention other things which he has done in the last year to aid the problem which is most serious to the fishing industry. Out on the west coast, and I am sure on the east coast as well, the actual job of catching the fish has been pretty well solved. The great problem is disposing of the fish in a good market. Before the war, of course, our British Columbia fishing industry had a very profitable European market. It is, however, agreed that here in Canada we could absorb pretty well our entire fish catch from both the east and west coasts if our consumption were anywhere near the consumption of fish of some of the European countries. As a matter of fact, as the minister pointed out, one of the reasons why we have not got that high consumption of fish is that it has been so difficult to get good fish into the central part of Canada where the big markets exist. The minister has done much more in this last year, as we of the fishing ridings know full well, than introduce a bill for the grading and inspecting of fish.
One of the great problems of course has been to transport fresh fish. The research branch of the Department of Fisheries has

done excellent work on mechanical refrigeration cars, cars which will take fish down to Winnipeg or Toronto. These cars have made trips now from the east coast to the west coast and from the west coast to the east coast, and the fish carried by them has arrived in perfect condition. Work is now going on in the development of modern cold storage plants. I think the one we have in Vancouver is a model for the entire nation. Other work has gone on into pickling and grading of fish, work which has been greatly helped by the research work done by the research department of fisheries on the west coast and, I imagine, on the east coast as well.
However, the great job in Canada as far as the fisheries are concerned is selling more of our very excellent fish from both the east and west coasts to the people of Canada across the whole ten provinces. In that regard I think the minister is well qualified to be the Minister of Fisheries at this time. Those of us from the west coast know that in his own private business he has been immensely successful in marketing his product across western Canada, including the prairie provinces. We who represent fishing ridings hope that he is going to be as successful marketing British Columbia fish across the prairie provinces as he has been in his own private life.

Mr. Speaker, it is a great pleasure for me to address the house on fisheries this evening. As I said before when speaking on this matter, fish and fishing are of prime importance to our newest province. I was interested in reading what I presume to be the last bulletin issued by the fisheries council of Canada. It is headed:
Prime Minister Pledges Government Support to Full Development of the Fisheries Potential.
It includes part of the address given by the Prime Minister (Mr. St. Laurent) to the fisheries council meeting in Ottawa on September 9, I believe. At that time the Prime Minister said:
The commercial fisheries implements the true significance of Canada's motto "From sea to sea."
He said that he thought that both federal and provincial governments could make profitable investments in the industry to improve and enlarge its output. He said:
Canadians can consume much more fish than they have in the past. When there is a domestic market it is a safe thing to rely on in trade. I hope the domestic market will provide increasing opportunities for the disposal of Canadian fish.
Then the Prime Minister added:
The federal government does not want to replace you, step into your field or become a competitor. But there are ways and means whereby the federal and provincial governments can contribute to the

further development of the industry. They have done so in the past but I feel there is room for more in the future. You can count on us for serious consideration to any recommendations of your council in the interest of the well-being of the whole Canadian economy.
I presume the Prime Minister meant the government. That was a most encouraging address of the Prime Minister, followed of course as it was by the various recommendations as contained in this official bulletin. I presume hon. members have received this bulletin. I do not imagine that they have all read it. On the second page we have this statement:
Prime Minister Backs Honourable Mayhew Announcing Government Policies.
There are some wonderful policies outlined in the bulletin. To the hon. members who have not read it I seriously suggest that it is their duty to do so, because fish and fishing are going to be increasingly more prominent in the affairs of this house than they have been in the past. I think the minister will agree with that statement as well.
When I spoke on this matter before, I made reference to the minister, and I should like to amplify my remarks. It is a great pleasure to do so. When I made my remarks before I did not know the full import of the visit that he made to Newfoundland in July of this year, but from the information I have obtained since, and I have obtained it from unimpeachable sources, I have learned that in July the minister, accompanied by his deputy and by his chief economist, visited the province. In the time at his disposal he made it his business to get every shade of opinion from the heads of industry right down to the fishermen themselves. I am told he spared no effort to obtain a full and complete picture in the time that he could spare to round out his knowledge of the fishing industry in Newfoundland. I can assure the house that the general impression created by the minister on that visit to Newfoundland was that he intended to understand the industry, so far as Newfoundland was concerned at least, from top to bottom. He spared no effort, and certainly did not spare himself in obtaining or endeavouring to obtain every possible fact that would aid him in guiding his department along the lines he intended to adopt in the future.
I am sure the minister will agree with me when I say how much the people of Newfoundland thought of his deputy minister, Dr. Bates, who accompanied him. While my knowledge of the fishing industry is not nearly as complete as that of the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay (Mr. Ashbourne), who is not now in his seat, or indeed as great as that of the Secretary of
Fish Inspection Act
State (Mr. Bradley), I am told that in the short time he was there Dr. Bates did a very thorough job in so far as organizing the Newfoundland fisheries department was concerned, and is continuing to do that job. I see the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay is now in his seat, and he will be able to amplify any remarks I have made concerning the minister and Dr. Bates.
I feel confident, with the interest the minister and his deputy have shown, and with their co-operation with the Newfoundland fisheries board, the province of Newfoundland has every reason to be satisfied with the future, in so far as the federal Department of Fisheries is concerned. I am certain the minister, his deputy and all the staff of the department are going to cooperate fully with the fisheries board and fishermen generally in Newfoundland. The fact that these gentlemen are showing such an obvious interest is a happy augury, so far as we of Newfoundland are concerned, for the future of our industry.
I hope I shall be pardoned for dealing generally with the bill, because I believe it is to be referred to a committee, and a complete discussion will take place there. There are however a few observations I should like to make now. The life of the Newfoundland fishermen, like the life of fishermen in the other maritime provinces, is no bed of roses. It is probably much easier in British Columbia where everything is perfect; but I can assure the house that in Newfoundland the fisherman's life is by no means perfect. He has to work long and hard hours, for which his returns are by no means great. The Secretary of State and the hon. member for Grand Falls-White Bay will know very well that the return for these long hours of hard labour is very small indeed. In fact if I were to make a guess at it-and my guess would not be a too well-informed one- I would say that, having paid for his supplies for the year, the average Newfoundland fisherman would be very fortunate if he had a return of any more than $400 or $500. That is my assumption-and even that amount is higher than it has been in the past. I know that what I shall now say is not within the purview of the bill now before us, but if it were possible in years like the present one, where many parts of Newfoundland have suffered from what we call blank years in fishing, and where a large number of our fishermen will have nothing to look forward to for the next six months, until the fisheries open up again, if there were something in the nature of the Prairie Farm Assistance Act, which was passed to assist prairie farmers in bad times, it would be a

Fish Inspection Act
very wonderful boon not only to the fishermen of Newfoundland but to all fishermen throughout this great dominion.
Dealing first with our own particular problems in the industry, I would turn first to salt codfish. Here the most important factor is that of the exchange situation and its effect upon our sales, and upon the sales of all maritimes fish in European markets. If a normal catch is to be marketed to the best advantage, it is necessary that half that catch be sold in Europe. This is not the problem of only one year; it is a continuous one. It may be that some hon. members are not thoroughly familiar with the manner in which our fish are now marketed. It means that the government of Newfoundland has had to put up dollars in London, and the sterling is converted in that way. It is not, as you will note, a condition which can continue forever, if the province has to arrange marketing in that way. Therefore I say it is a serious condition. Unless some arrangements are made for the convertibility of sterling it will mean that not only the Newfoundland fishery but indeed the whole fishing industry dealing in salt codfish will come crashing down around our ears. That is what will happen; there is no question about it.

Mr. Speaker, we have heard from British Columbia a number of times, from Newfoundland and indirectly from Prince Edward Island. I am rising because I do not see any other hon. members here from New Brunswick who represent

fishing constituencies, and I should like to say a few words on behalf of the fisheries of our province. I congratulate the minister on this bill, which I think will be received with general satisfaction in my province. When it goes to the committee I am sure there will be ample opportunity to discuss all its provisions.
I should like to point out one thing, however; that is, that while we may not be the greatest fishing province in the dominion, in the past we have had great interest in the fisheries of the country. Our province supplied three successive ministers of fisheries, but I was always amazed that in selecting a minister, instead of choosing one from some fishing constituency, a lawyer representing some inland constituency was usually chosen. Now, however, we have a minister who knows something about fishing, and the ministry of fisheries is no longer an orphan, as it was for fifteen years. In the past it was a sort of stepping-stone for ministers who were on their way to other and what might be termed more important portfolios. But the portfolio of fisheries is very important and is becoming more so; and I am sure that is realized by the present minister.
I want to point out that in New Brunswick we have the largest sardine factory in the world. I want to point out also that the smelt fisheries of New Brunswick are considered at least as good as, if not better than, any in this country. I would point out also that the oysters found in Northumberland strait are second to none in the world. Finally, and this was my reason for rising at this time, I want to mention the Saint John salmon. The hon. member for Queens-Shel-burne (Mr. Smith) and the hon. member for Cumberland (Mr. Black) mentioned that Atlantic salmon were superior to the British Columbia variety, but they did not specify, as they should, that Saint John harbour salmon are the finest to be found on the Atlantic seaboard. Hon. members from British Columbia said that British Columbia fish were the finest to be found anywhere, and tried to lead us to believe there were no poor fish in that province. Surely it would be taxing the credulity of hon. members too much to expect them to believe that statement.
I am sure that when this legislation goes to committee it will receive careful consideration. The hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. Higgins) brought out a point which I am sure interests and worries all of us; that is the matter of markets for our fish. I do not doubt the minister will see that the fish are packed as attractively as possible; we know we can produce the finest fish in the

world, but the great problem the government will have to consider is the finding of markets for these fish after they have been caught and placed in these splendid containers for which provision is made in this bill.

The minister has been here a long time, and he knows that when the session reaches a certain stage matters will be steamrollered through pretty rapidly. I should like to see the committee called as soon as possible, so that we may give this bill proper consideration.
Fish inspection is all right in its place, but it will not cure the ills of the fishing industry on either the east or the west coast. There are some defects in this bill. Representatives of the industry have submitted a brief to many members of this house pointing out changes that are necessary. I should like to see this bill passed at this session, so that the department can get on with the work the bill is designed to carry out. Can the minister give any assurance that he will arrange for the calling of the committee as soon as possible?

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRA VICTORIA, B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Since the representatives of all the provinces have had something to say, I think I might say a few words on behalf of the province of Prince Edward Island. I welcome this bill, and I am glad that the minister has told us it will be referred to a special committee of the house. A full opportunity will be given in the committee to go into the details of this measure. At the present time, of course, we need compulsory inspection, and not inspection in one place and not in another. However, the regulations as well as the bill itself can be dealt with in committee.
Fish Inspection Act
In closing my remarks, I should like to say that it was a pleasure for me, although sometimes slightly embarrassing, to hear the hon. members from the different provinces boasting of the qualities of their fish. I should like to draw your attention to the fish of Prince Edward Island. While the other hon. members have been fighting for second place in the quality of their fish, it is not necessary for me to say any more than to name the different varieties of fish from Prince Edward Island for all to agree that they are first in quality.
Let me first mention those delicious bivalves, the oysters. Prince Edward Island oysters have no superiors. Next, I shall mention our scallops. If one is so inclined one can taste these nearly every day at the evening meal in the parliamentary restaurant. The hon. member for Vancouver East (Mr. Maclnnis) led you to believe that the people of Prince Edward Island eat nothing but herring. I am sure you will agree with me that if we do, they are at least fattening, if I am any example.
In addition to herring, and before I mention anything else, let me speak of our lobsters. So far tonight nothing has been said about the superiority of the lobsters in other places. Our lobsters, owing to good regulations in the packing and fishing, have taken the top place in the markets of the world. I could go on to describe the wonderful mackerel, fresh or processed. They are fit for the table of a king. Our halibut and cod, likewise. Then, we come to the smelts. When I was mentioning shellfish, I might have mentioned that our clams and quahogs have a class and distinction of their own. If any of these products are marked with the words "Prince Edward Island product", they are accorded a place superior to any other.
I might also mention a provision in this bill concerning marine plants. The Irish moss industry in our province has been exceptionally flourishing because of the excellent quality of the product. Then, the buyers began to buy any quality without inspection and, as a consequence, the markets have somewhat soured on the product of the east and are turning back to the moss found in the Mediterranean. I might say that the regulations in connection with sea plants will be a help and a delight to those who participated in the Irish moss, kelp, dulce and seaweed industries. I wish to say again that, when the bill is in committee, I am sure all the good points will be brought out and we will probably be able to add some other beneficial provisions.

Fish Inspection Act
After all, we can regulate the fishing industry; we can tell people how to fish and how to process the fish; but if the industry is to survive, the thing it must have is markets for the various types of fish.

speakeroldname: Mr. T. G. W. Ashbourne (Grand Falls-Whiie Bay):
maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRA VICTORIA, B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I consider that this
legislative action will not only assist, but protect one of the important industries in the Canadian economy. As I said when this measure was introduced as a resolution, I consider it is a move in the right direction. I should like also to add my congratulations to those already given the Minister of Fisheries this evening.
Before this bill is given second reading, Mr. Speaker, I should like to avail myself of the opportunity of saying that I am in accord with the principle of this bill. It will be going to the special committee of this house, and no doubt there it will receive due consideration. I believe that the present trend is toward a closer watch over important industries such as fishing, and a recognition of the importance of producing clean, wholesome food. We can readily agree, I think, that constant vigilance is essential to ensure that the best possible article is produced, not only so that those participating in the industry can make a success of it but that the consumption of fish may be increased. I fear that oftentimes the high nutritive value of this product is either not generally understood or not fully recognized by those who purchase this important article of diet.
To ensure the maintenance of a suitable standard of excellence so that the product will enjoy the confidence of the public, I consider inspection a necessity. We know, Mr. Speaker, that for some time our competitors have had inspection of their fish. In certain countries, I understand, it is inspected right from the time it is taken out of the boat until it is exported. That is really a good idea. As we know, from the time a fish leaves the salt water or the fresh water, as the case may be, until it goes into consumption, there is a gradual process of deterioration. In order to protect the person who is to buy this fish and to see that he gets it in good condition, inspection is necessary. Naturally we want people to eat more fish. We know of its high protein value. Today being a fish day, I think it is an opportune time for this bill to be passed. By having a definite program of inspection, Mr. Speaker, I think that we shall be able to build up an industry which will give greater remuneration to the man who catches the fish and which will also in time aid in our Canadian economy.
Salmon was mentioned here this evening. We in Newfoundland pride ourselves upon the excellence of our salmon. In fact,
[Mr. McLure.I
Mr. Speaker, in the past, in the autumn of the year, we in Newfoundland have been getting twenty pound and twenty-five pound salmon, taken from the net, which were fit for a king; they were perfect. By looking after our salmon, our cod and every other source of food which can contribute to our people's well-being, I believe that we are assisting in the improvement of the general economy of the country and that, by so doing, our people will be able to enjoy these rich products of the sea which I think they sorely need.
There was a time when the people in Newfoundland used to eat a great deal of herring. I believe that the herring is one of the most important food fishes that we have. The act that was introduced and put upon the statute books in 1914 I believe had to do with the inspection of herring and other pickled fish. Some of the details embodied in this bill now before us were in that act at that time. As I said before, Mr. Speaker, I approve of the principle of the bill. Before the Newfoundland fisheries board was established and before we had any regular, definite government inspection there, there was a time in Newfoundland when the board of trade themselves furnished an inspection certificate with certain codfish which had to be exported. Naturally anyone who buys a perishable article such as codfish will have a greater sense of confidence when opening up credits, and when paying money against shipments, if he can count upon an effective system of inspection.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRA VICTORIA, B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
I wish to speak only briefly tonight, Mr. Speaker. Since this bill was introduced by the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Mayhew), it has been carefully studied by all hon. members from centres that are interested in fishing. I can assure you that I have looked it over carefully and that there are many clauses in the bill with which I do not agree. It has been discussed at great length among the members from New Brunswick, and I can speak for that province.
One criticism I have to offer in connection with this bill is that it gives to fisheries inspectors far more authority than I think it should give. We have today many young men who joined the fisheries department within the last two or three years and who perhaps have not the knowledge of the fishing industry that they will have at some future time. To give to them the authority that it is proposed to give them by this bill would, I believe, leave the department wide open to criticism.
When young men step in and tell older men who have been in the business for fifty or sixty years how they should run their busi-

ness, they are not met with open arms. With regard to the fishing industry, the agriculture industry or any other industry, my idea is that regimentation is not the solution to the problem. I believe that what we need in our fishing industry today are inspectors qualified to meet fishermen, to work with them and to be of assistance by reason of knowledge they might have which they could pass along to the fishermen. When you approach the matter in the other way and say that you must not do this and you must not do that, the fishermen resent it. I know that to be the fact. I have worked with them for many years. I do not believe you will find in Ottawa any officials to whom more authority is given to enforce regulations than is given in this bill to inspectors in connection with the inspection of fish.
Several hon. members have spoken of inspection and grading. I am much in favour of a better product in the fishing industry. If this industry is to survive, it will survive on quality. That should be the aim of every person who is interested in the industry. He should strive to improve the quality of the product. I believe that is right. But to date I believe the department has had the cart before the horse. Inspection should take place before the fish are ever taken from the boats.
To explain what I mean in a brief manner, let us take, for example, the sardine industry. A boat will come in loaded with sardines. The sardines are taken into the cannery, in which hundreds and hundreds of dollars are expended on labour. Hundreds of pounds of tin plate are used. Thousands of gallons of edible oil are used. After that process has been completed, the inspector will draw samples and tell you if the product is fit for human consumption or not. Why all this labour and all these materials should be wasted, I fail to understand. The inspectors with the fisheries department should be qualified to go aboard that boat at the cannery, inspect the fish there and follow them through until they are completely processed. Until we get a system of that sort, we are certainly going to be criticized by the people who are in the canning industry. I think we shall also be criticized by the general public because of the fact that good labour and good material are unnecessarily wasted.
Once more I want to emphasize my belief in quality. As I stated before, if this industry is to grow to the extent that we should like to see it grow, I believe this can be done only through quality. Fishermen are reasonable people. I worked with them for many years. They like to be advised, but they do not like to be pushed around. Fishermen are an intelligent group. As young men they started 45781-81i
Fish Inspection Act
out to work for themselves; they have never worked for somebody else for wages; they have always been out on their own. To that extent I would say that they are perhaps a little bit more independent than the ordinary person you meet. They are reasonable if they are talked to in their own language; but they are stubborn if you start to push them around. There is one other clause in this bill that I want to mention briefly. It is in connection with fish that may be seized by an inspector.

maintopic: PROVINCIAL LIBRA VICTORIA, B. C. HOUSE OF COMMONS
speechtext:
Today fisheries inspectors have great authority and if they suspect there might be something wrong with certain types of fish they can seize them. They have authority to hold them for a period of two months. I often wonder, in regard to fresh fish, live lobsters, shellfish and anything of that kind, just what condition they would be in after an inspector had held them for two months. Again I wonder if they were put in cold storage and kept there for two months who would be responsible for the cold storage charges. It is matters of this kind that are bothering the fishermen and men connected with the fishing industry today.
What I should like to see the Department of Fisheries do, and some day I hope they will do it, is to take these young men whom they have in their employ and teach them to the point where they will be able to go out with the fishermen and be helpful. Instead of being a police officer, be a teacher. When we get that sort of set-up in our fisheries department I believe that they will be doing a lot to encourage the fishing industry.
As I said before, these young men are honest; they are fine boys; they are conscientious; but their knowledge of the fishing industry is limited. They have not had the experience. A course of two or three weeks in any part of the Dominion of Canada would not give them sufficient knowledge to go out into the industry today and try to help those engaged in the industry. I do hope that the department will seriously consider the suggestion that instead of an official being a police officer he should go out to assist the industry. May I give one example. In my own province we have a provincial fisheries department. It is very small. There are only two or three in that department. We have one young man there today who has had a lot of experience in the fisheries of our province. For example, some fishermen will rig up a trawler and go trawling. They will go out, drag for several days, and their equip-

Fish Inspection Act
ment will not work properly. There is something wrong. The fisherman cannot find out what it is. He calls this young man. I have known him to go out and stay out for four or five days in the bay of Fundy with these men until he found where the trouble was, and rectified it for them. He has gone to different places in the province where they have problems and he has been of great assistance to the fishermen. Today this young man is held in high regard. When we find other inspectors with the federal department who are as qualified and are willing to go out and assist men in the business we shall find little criticism from the fishermen. But as long as the department takes the attitude that it is a police department, that you have got a tough bunch to work with, just so long will these men resent that fact and, I fear, perhaps co-operate less than if they were treated as men are treated in other industries in this country.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I have very few words to utter in this chamber tonight. I would describe this house tonight as a house of the east and the west. We had the
hon. member for Nanaimo (Mr. Pearkes) telling us that fish in British Columbia was superb. It would seem to be so from the fact that the regulations do not apply to them. It would also seem that the fishing industry should be a model for the fruit industry, because when we were discussing the fruit industry we found that it was not quite perfect.
In regard to the regulations for inspection of lobsters, we heard the hon. member for Charlotte (Mr. Stuart) saying that assistance of an educational nature was the most important, and not so much inspection. The inspectors should be educators. I believe it is the intention of the department to have the men go around and help teach the fishermen the right way to do things. We found that when co-operative methods were introduced in the lobster business in Newfoundland it was the most beneficial thing that had happened to the lobster industry in the whole history of that province. The value of the lobster to the fishermen increased tremendously. We have to get fishermen into the organization. The minister knows that at present the codfishing industry is controlled by the fisheries board and the merchants. It costs $10,000 to join the fish merchants export association. What I want to point out is that the fisherman has not yet been given the position that he should have in this whole picture. I would suggest to the minister that he give consideration to the appointment of a representative of the fishermen themselves on the fisheries council, or on whatever body is to be in charge.

Mr. Speaker, I have no intention of delaying the house or delaying the second reading of this bill, but I do want to answer the hon.

member for Cape Breton South (Mr. Gillis) about the date of the meeting. I have not the setting of the date of the meeting, but I think there will be ample time for the committee on marine and fisheries to have a meeting a week from Monday. There will also be ample time for anyone from any part of Canada to get here who may want to come. Again it will give us time to give the bill all the study it deserves and get it back into the house to have third reading before the house prorogues.
There are several things that I should like to say, but I think I shall have time to say them on the estimates. I do not want to get into a discussion tonight on whether the best fish are to be found on the east coast or the west coast. I think we have starfish at both places. When this bill is in operation-and it will probably take a year before it is in operation-it will mean, I think, a quality of fish better than anything we have had before. Quality in fish is the selling point-and sales regulate any business with which I have ever been connected. I believe if we can get quality in our fish there will be no difficulty in getting sales. We have the greatest potential cold-water fisheries in the world and we can make this industry one of which Canada will be proud.
We cannot pay too much attention to the development of our fisheries, our forests, our farms, our mines-indeed all our natural resources-and the maximum attention will be paid to our fisheries.
When the estimates are before the committee I shall answer all the questions which have been put to me. I have here the answers to the questions asked on Thursday night by the hon. member for St. John's East, but those answers will require some time. Perhaps he would be content if I were to put them on record when we are considering the estimates, on the understanding that he may have them in the meantime if he wishes.
